AI.method: Combines trajectory optimization (accounting for internal eMNS dynamics) with time-varying Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) state feedback and Iterative Learning Control (ILC) that refines feedforward commands using previous trial data and the system's dynamic model.
AI.result: ILC enables successful swing-up within six iterations, whereas LQR alone fails. Post-experimental analysis shows the learned ILC correction closely matches torque discrepancy predicted by high-fidelity magnetic field model calibration.
AI.conclusion: Learning and adaptation (specifically ILC) is a promising tool to handle uncertainties in electromagnetic actuation, such as patient-specific physiological motion patterns and field model calibration inaccuracies. The method is applicable to other magnetically actuated devices like catheters and guidewires.

title: A Multi-Agent AI System for Automated High School Transcript Processing: Collaborative Document Analysis at Scale
summary: Each year, college admissions offices face an overwhelming challenge: processing millions of high school transcripts, each with unique formats, grading systems, and layouts. This manual process creates operational bottlenecks that delay admissions decisions and consume valuable resources. We present a transformative solution through a multi-agent AI system where specialized agents collaborate to automatically process diverse transcript formats through intelligent coordination and communication. Our multi-agent architecture consists of three specialized agents-a Pattern Recognition Agent for format-specific parsing, a Semantic Analysis Agent for natural language understanding, and a Vision Intelligence Agent for multimodal document analysis-coordinated by an Orchestration Agent that manages agent communication and result reconciliation. Our key innovation lies in agent-based quality control using GPA extraction as a coordination signal, ensuring reliable agent collaboration and preventing critical information loss. When evaluated on 40 real world transcripts from high schools across 13 U.S. states, our agent system successfully processed every document, achieving 96.7% accuracy compared to expert manual review while maintaining practical processing speeds of 45 seconds per transcript. This work demonstrates how multi-agent coordination can solve complex document processing challenges, offering institutions a scalable, collaborative AI solution that preserves accuracy while dramatically reducing processing time.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent AI system with three specialized agents (Pattern Recognition, Semantic Analysis, Vision Intelligence) coordinated by an Orchestration Agent automates college transcript processing, achieving 96.7% accuracy on 40 real transcripts from 13 U.S. states at 45 seconds per transcript.
AI.motivation: College admissions offices face operational bottlenecks from manually processing millions of diverse high school transcripts with unique formats, grading systems, and layouts, delaying admissions decisions and consuming valuable resources.
AI.method: A multi-agent architecture with three specialized agents (Pattern Recognition Agent for format-specific parsing, Semantic Analysis Agent for natural language understanding, Vision Intelligence Agent for multimodal document analysis) coordinated by an Orchestration Agent that manages communication and result reconciliation, with agent-based quality control using GPA extraction as a coordination signal.
AI.result: Successfully processed all 40 real transcripts from high schools across 13 U.S. states, achieving 96.7% accuracy compared to expert manual review with practical processing speeds of 45 seconds per transcript.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent coordination can solve complex document processing challenges, offering institutions a scalable, collaborative AI solution that preserves accuracy while dramatically reducing processing time.

title: An Attention-based Model for Robust Forecasting with Missing Modality
summary: Learning with missing modalities is a fundamental challenge in multimodal robot learning, as real-world robotic systems often operate in environments with incomplete sensor data. Attention-based models are appealing for processing multimodal data because they can handle multiple modalities with a single backbone network. However, most multimodal models assume that all modalities are available during both training and inference, limiting their applicability in robotic perception and decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a multimodal model designed to handle missing modalities during both training and inference. The model is formulated as a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) and incorporates a transformer-based architecture that leverages attention mechanisms to learn a unified, fixed-dimensional representation, even when some modalities are missing. We show that our proposed model can be trained with missing modalities while approximating a robust representation of all modalities. We evaluate our approach on five multimodal datasets across two robot learning tasks: human trajectory prediction and robot manipulation forecasting. Experimental results demonstrate that our model effectively learns from incomplete data and is superior to prior multimodal fusion approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a multimodal model based on a conditional variational autoencoder with transformer attention that can handle missing modalities during both training and inference, demonstrating superior performance on robot learning tasks like human trajectory prediction and manipulation forecasting.
AI.motivation: Real-world robotic systems often suffer from incomplete sensor data, yet most multimodal models assume all modalities are available during training and inference, limiting their applicability in robotic perception and decision-making.
AI.method: The model is formulated as a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) with a transformer-based architecture that uses attention mechanisms to learn a unified, fixed-dimensional representation even when some modalities are missing. It supports missing modalities during both training and inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on five multimodal datasets across two robot learning tasks (human trajectory prediction and robot manipulation forecasting), the model effectively learns from incomplete data and outperforms prior multimodal fusion approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CVAE-transformer model robustly handles missing modalities, approximates a complete multimodal representation, and achieves superior performance in robot learning tasks compared to existing fusion methods.

title: Sorries Are Not the Hard Part: An Expert-Review Case Study of a Semi-Autonomous Formalization
summary: Large language models can often close proof gaps in interactive theorem provers, but a verified theorem is not the same thing as a reusable library contribution. We study this distinction through a detailed case study: a semi-autonomous formalization of Grothendieck's vanishing theorem. The initial version compiles with no sorries, but an expert review found serious problems in definitions, theorem generality, file organization, and the API. We then ran a review-driven refactor and compression process and obtained a second expert review. The before-and-after comparison shows a sharp split: agents adapted well to local, mechanically checkable feedback, but remained weak at choosing definitions and designing APIs. We argue that autoformalization should be evaluated not only by closed sorries, but by whether the resulting formalization survives expert review.

AI.tldr: This case study on formalizing Grothendieck's vanishing theorem reveals that while LLMs can close proof gaps in interactive theorem provers, the resulting formalizations often fail expert review due to poor definitions, API design, and file organization, suggesting autoformalization should be evaluated by expert review survival rather than just compiling without errors.
AI.motivation: To highlight the gap between verified theorems (that compile) and reusable library contributions, and to argue that autoformalization evaluation should go beyond mechanical checking to include expert review.
AI.method: A detailed case study of semi-autonomous formalization of Grothendieck's vanishing theorem, followed by a review-driven refactor and compression process with two rounds of expert review for before-and-after comparison.
AI.result: Initial version compiled with no sorries but had serious problems in definitions, theorem generality, file organization, and API. Agents handled local, mechanically checkable feedback well but were weak at choosing definitions and designing APIs.
AI.conclusion: Autoformalization should be evaluated not only by closed sorries (compilation success) but by whether the formalization survives expert review.

title: SplatlessDF: Continuous Distance Field Mapping with Non-Splatting Gaussians
summary: Recent Gaussian splatting (GS) methods have shown that scenes can be represented efficiently with optimisable Gaussians for high-quality reconstruction and rendering. In this paper, building on this principle, we introduce SplatlessDF, a continuous distance field (DF) mapping framework that uses anisotropic Gaussian elements from a spatial rather than photometric perspective. SplatlessDF directly parameterises the Gaussians and optimises to recover a differentiable DF, enabling distances and gradients to be queried in the spatial domain for downstream robotic tasks such as navigation. Furthermore, SplatlessDF can be coupled with 2D Gaussian splatting (2DGS), providing a unified framework based solely on Gaussian primitives that can learn continuous DF and surface models and supports photometric rendering. We consider two settings: a standalone DF-only formulation and a joint DF-rendering formulation coupled with 2DGS. Experiments show that the standalone formulation provides efficient and accurate distance and gradient queries, while the joint formulation improves rendering geometry and simultaneously models a continuous DF. These results highlight the potential of GS-style representations not only for surface modelling and rendering but also for mapping representations suited to robotic navigation.

AI.tldr: SplatlessDF uses anisotropic Gaussian elements to learn a continuous distance field from a spatial perspective, supporting both standalone DF mapping and joint DF-rendering with 2D Gaussian splatting for robotic navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing Gaussian splatting methods focus on photometric rendering; this work extends them to model continuous distance fields for robotic navigation, enabling distance and gradient queries in spatial domains.
AI.method: SplatlessDF parameterizes anisotropic Gaussians and optimizes them to recover a differentiable distance field. It offers two formulations: a standalone DF-only setting and a joint DF-rendering formulation coupled with 2D Gaussian splatting.
AI.result: Standalone formulation yields efficient and accurate distance and gradient queries; joint formulation improves rendering geometry while simultaneously modeling a continuous DF.
AI.conclusion: GS-style representations are promising not only for surface modeling and rendering but also for mapping representations suited to robotic navigation.

title: Adversarial Concept Search: Predicting Compositional Errors From Feature Geometry
summary: Humans cannot always intuit what scenarios are most challenging to LLMs. Hoping to capture challenging edge cases, developers either design problems to be difficult for humans or curate extensive benchmarks. What if we could instead anticipate which scenarios a model will fail on? In this paper, we use an LLM's representational geometry to predict which concept combinations it will fail on. We attribute this compositional failure to interference between salient features. In tasks that require systematic composition - toy programmatic settings, multihop reasoning, multilingual factual recall - we find that when a pair of concepts is encoded near-orthogonally, the model reliably composes them. When their linear encodings are close, producing interference, the model fails to compose them. Our method reliably anticipates failure modes across different compositional tasks, without evaluating specific inputs. These results lay the groundwork to use representational geometry to identify high-risk examples, construct targeted stress tests, and provide a scalable foundation for active learning in real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper uses an LLM's representational geometry to predict compositional failures. When concept encodings are near-orthogonal, models compose them reliably; when encodings interfere (are close), models fail. This method anticipates failure modes without evaluating specific inputs.
AI.motivation: Humans cannot reliably intuit which scenarios will be most challenging for LLMs, and existing approaches rely on manually designing difficult problems or curating large benchmarks. The authors aim to instead proactively anticipate failure cases using the model's own internal representations.
AI.method: The authors analyze the representational geometry of LLMs, specifically measuring the angle between linear encodings of concept pairs. They attribute compositional failures to interference between salient features. They test the method across toy programmatic settings, multihop reasoning, and multilingual factual recall tasks.
AI.result: When concept pairs are encoded near-orthogonally, the model reliably composes them. When their linear encodings are close (producing interference), the model fails to compose them. This method reliably anticipates failure modes across different compositional tasks without evaluating specific inputs.
AI.conclusion: Representational geometry can be used to identify high-risk examples, construct targeted stress tests, and provide a scalable foundation for active learning in real-world LLM deployment.

title: From Attacks to Curricula: Learnability-Guided Adversarial Training for Safe Autonomous Driving
summary: Closed-loop adversarial training improves autonomous driving safety by exposing policies to rare safety-critical scenarios. Standard pipelines first generate adversarial scenarios and then sample them for policy optimization. However, most existing frameworks remain attack-oriented: collision-driven generators often synthesize unsolvable extreme situations, which can degrade learning, while heuristic samplers ignore the evolving capability of the driving policy, causing sample inefficiency and delayed convergence. We propose AlignADV, a learnability-guided closed-loop adversarial training framework that converts adversarial scenarios into resolvable and capability-aligned curricula. First, we reformulate adversarial scenario generation as a preference alignment problem and employ direct preference optimization to guide the generator toward critical yet resolvable scenarios. Second, we introduce behavioral fingerprints to capture the intrinsic characteristics of the evolving policy and construct a multi-modal capability prediction model that estimates policy performance without expensive closed-loop simulations. By combining resolvability-aligned scenarios with capability predictions, AlignADV develops a dynamic curriculum sampling mechanism that prioritizes scenarios targeting the current policy's vulnerabilities. Experiments on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset demonstrate that AlignADV improves convergence efficiency and final performance, reducing training steps by up to 40.6 percent compared with baseline methods while lowering collision rate and improving route completion under both normal and adversarial traffic conditions. These results highlight a shift from attack-oriented scenario generation to learnability-guided policy improvement, offering a principled direction for safer and more efficient autonomous driving training. Project page: https://meiyuewen.github.io/AlignADV/.

AI.tldr: AlignADV is a learnability-guided closed-loop adversarial training framework for autonomous driving that converts adversarial scenarios into resolvable, capability-aligned curricula using preference-aligned scenario generation, behavioral fingerprints, and dynamic curriculum sampling, achieving 40.6% fewer training steps and improved safety.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial training pipelines are attack-oriented: collision-driven generators produce unsolvable extreme scenarios that degrade learning, and heuristic samplers ignore the evolving policy's capability, causing sample inefficiency and slow convergence.
AI.method: (1) Reformulates adversarial scenario generation as a preference alignment problem using direct preference optimization to produce critical yet resolvable scenarios. (2) Introduces behavioral fingerprints to capture evolving policy characteristics and builds a multi-modal capability prediction model to estimate policy performance without costly closed-loop simulations. (3) Combines resolvability-aligned scenarios with capability predictions to develop a dynamic curriculum sampling mechanism that prioritizes scenarios targeting current policy vulnerabilities.
AI.result: On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, AlignADV reduces training steps by up to 40.6% compared to baselines, lowers collision rate, and improves route completion under both normal and adversarial traffic conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights a shift from attack-oriented scenario generation to learnability-guided policy improvement, offering a principled direction for safer and more efficient autonomous driving training.

title: Minim: Privacy-Aware Minimal View for Agents via Trusted Local Sanitization
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 (43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea). Code available at https://github.com/yyyyhx/MINIM
summary: Modern LLM-powered autonomous agents increasingly rely on rich user interface (UI) state observations to achieve reliable action grounding in complex digital environments. However, many deployments transmit the full UI state to remote inference servers even when most elements are irrelevant to the current task, which can leak sensitive but unnecessary context such as authentication codes, private notifications, and background application states. We propose MINIM, a trusted local broker that performs privacy-aware minimization on the client side before any observation leaves the device. Grounded in Contextual Integrity (CI), MINIM learns a dual-score representation for each UI element by predicting an inherent sensitivity score (s) and a task-conditioned necessity score (n). These scores drive a ternary disclosure policy that keeps essential elements, abstracts sensitive attributes when needed, and removes task-irrelevant content. We optimize a CI-aware objective that penalizes necessity errors more strongly on high-risk content, enabling aggressive pruning while preserving task-critical information. Experiments on real-world UI observations derived from WebArena show that MINIM substantially reduces task-irrelevant sensitive leakage while preserving task-critical semantic context and the interactive affordances required for reliable agent actions.

AI.tldr: MINIM is a trusted local broker that performs privacy-aware minimization of UI state observations on the client side before sending them to remote inference servers. It uses a dual-score system (sensitivity and necessity) grounded in Contextual Integrity to selectively keep, abstract, or remove UI elements, reducing sensitive leakage while preserving task-critical information.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered autonomous agents transmit full UI states (including sensitive but irrelevant content like authentication codes, private notifications, background apps) to remote servers, causing privacy leakage.
AI.method: MINIM uses a dual-score representation (sensitivity score s, task-conditioned necessity score n) for each UI element, grounded in Contextual Integrity. A ternary disclosure policy keeps essential elements, abstracts sensitive attributes, and removes task-irrelevant content. A CI-aware objective penalizes necessity errors more heavily on high-risk content.
AI.result: Experiments on WebArena UI observations show MINIM substantially reduces task-irrelevant sensitive leakage while preserving task-critical semantic context and interactive affordances for agent actions.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-aware client-side UI minimization using CI-grounded dual-score prediction and ternary disclosure can effectively reduce privacy leakage without degrading autonomous agent task performance.

title: ReactSim-Bench: Benchmarking Reactive Behavior World Model Simulation in Autonomous Driving
summary: Reactive capability is a key property of data-driven behavior world model simulators for autonomous driving simulation systems. With this capability, simulated world agents can respond feasibly to autonomous vehicle (AV) behaviors that differ from the log. However, existing behavior simulation benchmarks do not directly measure reactive capability. They often let the simulator jointly control the AV and surrounding agents and evaluate realism through log similarity or open-loop prediction metrics. In this work, we introduce ReactSim-Bench for evaluating the reactive capability of behavior world model simulation in autonomous driving. We decouple the control of agents and the AV, using AV behaviors that differ from the log and require agents to respond as independent AV inputs. To obtain these AV behaviors, we construct a pipeline that uses an AV planner model to generate candidate behaviors and filters the data using rules and manual verification. Collision metrics, map-based metrics, and kinematic feasibility metrics are used to evaluate the safety and rule compliance of reactive responses. We construct 2,636 test scenarios with three categories and conduct a systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art models across multiple architectures, including Transformer-based, diffusion-based, and next-token-prediction-based models. We further analyze how replan frequency affects performance and provide insights for future studies.

AI.tldr: Introduces ReactSim-Bench, a benchmark to measure reactive capability of behavior world models in autonomous driving, decoupling AV and agent control to evaluate how well agents respond to realistic AV behaviors.
AI.motivation: Existing behavior simulation benchmarks do not directly measure reactive capability—they often jointly control AV and agents, evaluating realism via log similarity or open-loop prediction, failing to assess whether agents can feasibly respond to AV behaviors that differ from logged data.
AI.method: Decouples agent and AV control; uses an AV planner to generate candidate behaviors deviating from logs, filtered by rules and manual verification. Evaluates safety/rule compliance via collision, map-based, and kinematic feasibility metrics across 2,636 scenarios.
AI.result: Systematically evaluated Transformer-based, diffusion-based, and next-token-prediction-based models; analyzed impact of replan frequency on performance.
AI.conclusion: ReactSim-Bench provides a targeted benchmark for reactive capability, offering insights into model behavior under varied AV inputs and replan strategies for future research.

title: Formalizing Numerical Analysis: An Agent Pipeline and Quality Audit Beyond Kernel Acceptance
summary: Recent work has demonstrated that coding agents can formalize entire advanced mathematics textbooks in Lean 4, yet existing efforts concentrate on branches of mathematics already well-represented in mathlib and measure success solely through kernel acceptance. We address both limitations by applying a coding agent to formalize Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations, a textbook in numerical analysis that is largely absent from mathlib, stressing the agent's capacity to develop new theory from scratch. We further introduce a systematic, reproducible three-dimensional framework for evaluating the quality of agent-produced formalizations beyond compilation: semantic correctness, Mathlib reuse, and cross-file reuse via LLM-as-judge methods. Applying this framework to our own formalization and to the released outputs of RepoProver and M2F, we uncover recurring unfaithful formalization patterns, including incomplete multi-part statements, added weakening hypotheses, and parameter restrictions, that kernel acceptance entirely obscures. Our results suggest that compilation-based metrics substantially overstate formalization quality, and we provide a reproducible audit methodology to support more rigorous evaluation of future autoformalization systems.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses limitations in autoformalization research by applying a coding agent to formalize a numerical analysis textbook absent from mathlib, and introduces a three-dimensional evaluation framework (semantic correctness, Mathlib reuse, cross-file reuse via LLM-as-judge) that reveals compilation-based metrics significantly overstate formalization quality.
AI.motivation: Existing autoformalization efforts focus on math branches already well-represented in mathlib and evaluate success solely by kernel compilation acceptance, lacking assessment of formalization quality and missing the challenge of developing theory from scratch in under-represented domains.
AI.method: Applied a coding agent to formalize a numerical analysis textbook (Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations) largely absent from mathlib. Developed a three-dimensional evaluation framework measuring semantic correctness, Mathlib reuse, and cross-file reuse via LLM-as-judge methods. Applied this framework to their own formalization and to outputs from RepoProver and M2F.
AI.result: Identified recurring unfaithful formalization patterns (incomplete multi-part statements, added weakening hypotheses, parameter restrictions) that kernel compilation acceptance entirely obscures. Compilation-based metrics substantially overstate formalization quality.
AI.conclusion: Compilation-based metrics are insufficient for evaluating autoformalization quality; the proposed three-dimensional framework and reproducible audit methodology support more rigorous evaluation of future autoformalization systems.

title: Semidefinite Relaxations for Collision-Free Motion Planning
summary: We study semidefinite relaxations for collision-free motion planning. We focus on a point robot moving from start to goal through spherical obstacles in $\mathbb{R}^n$, subject to path continuity constraints and squared derivative costs; a setting that is conceptually simple yet captures the hardness of collision-free motion planning. We formulate this problem exactly as a nonconvex problem over polynomial curves, and present a natural semidefinite relaxation. We contribute two key theoretical insights; to our knowledge this is the first theoretical analysis of semidefinite relaxations for collision-free motion planning. First, we show that solving the convex relaxation is equivalent to solving, to global optimality, a related motion planning problem in a potentially higher-dimensional space. This geometric interpretation yields necessary and sufficient conditions for tightness, and a clear intuition for when the relaxation is loose. Second, we show that the relaxation admits a symmetry reduction that makes it significantly smaller than one might expect, with positive semidefinite cone sizes that scale linearly with the polynomial degree and are independent of the ambient dimension. The resulting relaxation is 10 to 100 times faster than direct nonlinear programming transcriptions solved with SNOPT and IPOPT, exhibits significantly lower variance in solve times, and reliably finds a locally optimal path for the original problem. We demonstrate its effectiveness as a convex steering function in an RRT planner for minimum-snap quadrotor planning with $C^4$ continuous trajectories.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and theoretically analyzes semidefinite relaxations for collision-free motion planning, showing they are equivalent to global planning in higher dimensions, admit efficient symmetry reduction, and outperform standard nonlinear solvers by 10-100x.
AI.motivation: To provide the first theoretical analysis of semidefinite relaxations for collision-free motion planning, addressing the hardness of this problem with convex optimization tools.
AI.method: Formulates collision-free motion planning as a nonconvex polynomial optimization problem, then develops a semidefinite relaxation. Provides two theoretical contributions: (1) geometric interpretation linking the convex relaxation to higher-dimensional motion planning with tightness conditions, (2) symmetry reduction yielding SDP cone sizes linear in polynomial degree and independent of ambient dimension.
AI.result: The relaxation is 10-100x faster than direct NLP transcriptions solved with SNOPT/IPOPT with lower variance, reliably finds locally optimal paths, and works effectively as a convex steering function in RRT for minimum-snap quadrotor planning with C4 continuous trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Semidefinite relaxations are both theoretically grounded and practically efficient for collision-free motion planning, with tightness conditions derived from geometric interpretations and substantial computational speedups.

title: Applicability Condition Extraction for Therapeutic Drug-Disease Relations
summary: Identifying conditions that a certain drug takes therapeutic effect on a target disease is crucial for clinical decision-making support. However, most existing biomedical information extraction methods have focused on identifying only relations between drugs and diseases, while largely overlooking the context-specific conditions where such relations can apply. To address this problem, we introduce the task of applicability condition extraction for therapeutic drug--disease relations from biomedical research literature. We create the first dataset that has manually annotated triples of drugs, diseases, and applicability conditions on biomedical paper abstracts with 1,119 drug-disease pairs. Using this dataset, we systematically evaluate the performance of a range of existing methods. In addition, we propose a new method that enhances LoRA to consider relations between drugs and diseases. Our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across different evaluation settings. The source code and dataset of this paper can be obtained from: https://github.com/guantingluo98/Drug-ACE

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the task of applicability condition extraction for therapeutic drug-disease relations from biomedical literature, creates a manually annotated dataset of 1,119 drug-disease pairs with applicability conditions, evaluates existing methods, and proposes an enhanced LoRA method that outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing biomedical information extraction methods focus on identifying relations between drugs and diseases but overlook the context-specific conditions (applicability conditions) where such therapeutic relations apply. This gap limits clinical decision-making support.
AI.method: Created the first manually annotated dataset of drug-disease-applicability condition triples (1,119 drug-disease pairs) from biomedical paper abstracts. Proposed an enhanced LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) method that incorporates drug-disease relational information.
AI.result: The proposed LoRA-enhanced method consistently outperforms strong baselines across different evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: The task of applicability condition extraction is introduced and a new method leveraging enhanced LoRA with drug-disease relation awareness shows superior performance, with code and dataset publicly available.

title: Development of a 3 in Sewer Pipe Inspection Robot with an Articulated Differential Mechanism using X-shaped Linkages
comment: The 23rd International Conference on Ubiquitous Robots (UR 2026), 15-18 July, Osaka Ibaraki Campus, Ritsumeikan University, Ibaraki, Osaka, Japan
summary: This paper proposes, an improved version of the 3 in sewer pipe inspection robot equipped with an emergency evacuation mechanism. The low traction force and poor stepover capability, which were challenges of the first version, have been improved by simply connecting the propulsion units. The coupled propulsion units feature a differential mechanism capable of posture changes via a single wire, enabling adaptation to pipe diameter variations. To traverse obstacles like pipe joints, a control method was devised that detects obstacle contact through current load on the drive wheel motors and slackens the wire. This method was verified through simulated pipe experiments. Load comparisons were made using current waveforms applied to the drive wheels. Our proposed control method significantly improved the step-over capability of the new articulated robots.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an improved articulated sewer pipe inspection robot with a coupled propulsion unit and differential mechanism, improving traction and step-over capability through a control method that detects obstacles via motor current load and slackens a wire to adapt.
AI.motivation: To address the low traction force and poor stepover capability limitations of the first version of the 3-segment in-sewer pipe inspection robot.
AI.method: Improved the robot by connecting propulsion units with a differential mechanism that enables posture changes via a single wire, and developed a control method that detects obstacle contact through drive wheel motor current load to slacken the wire.
AI.result: Simulated pipe experiments verified the proposed control method; load comparisons using current waveforms demonstrated significantly improved step-over capability of the new articulated robot.
AI.conclusion: The proposed control method effectively enhances step-over capability of articulated sewer inspection robots, addressing the key limitations of the earlier version.

title: FactoryLLM: A Safe and Open-Source AI Playground for Evaluating LLMs in Smart Factories
summary: Fault diagnostics and recovery in smart factories is challenging because critical information is dispersed across manuals of multiple machines which are interconnected through the manufacturing process. Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide a promising approach. In this paper, we propose FactoryLLM, a safe and open-source AI playground designed for evaluating different LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models by analysing documents from multiple machines across the manufacturing process. FactoryLLM enables the user to configure the LLM, and assess performance when reasoning over multiple documents, through a dual evaluation setup using both RAGAS and NVIDIA's LLM-as-a-Judge metrics. FactoryLLM is safe because it allows users to run local or open-source LLMs without sharing sensitive industrial data, providing a controlled environment for experimentation. We demonstrate the efficacy of FactoryLLM through a case study which involves an Autonomous Intelligent Vehicle and its Mobile Planner software, evaluating three LLMs across 30 maintenance queries derived from approximately 600 pages of cross-machine documentation. The results suggest that FactoryLLM is effective in cross-machine document reasoning: every model achieved a groundedness score above 0.88. The full code and documentation for community to test FactoryLLM with their manufacturing specific scenarios are publicly available.

AI.tldr: FactoryLLM is an open-source AI playground for evaluating LLM-based RAG models on cross-machine document reasoning in smart factories, achieving groundedness scores above 0.88 across 30 maintenance queries from ~600 pages of documentation.
AI.motivation: Fault diagnostics and recovery in smart factories is challenging because critical information is dispersed across manuals of multiple interconnected machines; existing approaches lack safe, open-source tools for evaluating LLM-based RAG models on cross-machine document reasoning.
AI.method: FactoryLLM provides a configurable platform where users can select local/open-source LLMs, perform retrieval-augmented generation over multi-machine documentation, and evaluate performance using a dual setup of RAGAS and NVIDIA's LLM-as-a-Judge metrics.
AI.result: In a case study with an Autonomous Intelligent Vehicle and Mobile Planner software, three LLMs were evaluated on 30 maintenance queries from ~600 pages of cross-machine documentation; all models achieved a groundedness score above 0.88.
AI.conclusion: FactoryLLM is effective for cross-machine document reasoning in smart factory fault diagnostics, providing a safe, open-source playground for experimentation without sharing sensitive industrial data.

title: The N2D Haptic Glove: A Multi-Finger Glove for 2D Directional Force Feedback for Contact Rich Manipulation
summary: Humans rely on directional fingertip forces to probe and regulate contact during manipulation, yet most wearable haptic gloves render only vibration or single-axis force, leaving force direction ambiguous. Without directional cues, users must infer contact force from vision alone, often leading to over-pressing, inconsistent control, and reduced precision in robotic teleoperation. We present the N2D Haptic Glove, a multi-finger wearable device that renders planar flexion-extension fingertip forces using capstan-drive transmissions for high-transparency force feedback. Through benchtop validations and a user study involving haptic teleoperation of a robotic arm and hand, we demonstrate that compared to visual-only and single-axis haptic baselines, planar fingertip feedback significantly reduces contact force error during precise manipulation, improves trial-to-trial consistency, and enhances overall user experience in axial probing tasks. These findings establish the N2D Haptic Glove and directional finger-based haptics devices as a promising modality for contact-rich teleoperation, immersive virtual reality simulations, and robot learning from demonstrations. N2D Haptic Glove's hardware and software system will be fully open-sourced at \href{https://ucsdarclab.github.io/n2d-glove/}{this https URL}.

AI.tldr: The N2D Haptic Glove renders planar fingertip forces using capstan-drive transmissions, significantly reducing contact force error and improving consistency in robotic teleoperation compared to visual-only or single-axis haptic feedback.
AI.motivation: Humans rely on directional fingertip forces for manipulation, but existing haptic gloves only render vibration or single-axis force, leaving force direction ambiguous. This forces users to infer contact force from vision alone, causing over-pressing, inconsistent control, and reduced precision in teleoperation.
AI.method: Designed a multi-finger wearable haptic glove using capstan-drive transmissions to render planar flexion-extension fingertip forces with high transparency. Validated through benchtop tests and a user study comparing planar haptic feedback against visual-only and single-axis haptic baselines in teleoperated robotic arm and hand tasks.
AI.result: Planar fingertip feedback significantly reduced contact force error during precise manipulation, improved trial-to-trial consistency, and enhanced user experience in axial probing tasks compared to visual-only and single-axis haptic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Directional finger-based haptics (N2D Haptic Glove) is a promising modality for contact-rich teleoperation, immersive VR simulations, and robot learning from demonstrations. Hardware and software will be fully open-sourced.

title: VeriGeo: Controllable Geometry Question Generation with Numerical and Analytical Verification
summary: Geometry problem generation is useful for AI-assisted education and multimodal mathematical reasoning, but reliable synthesis remains difficult because the problem statement, diagram, constraints, and solution should be mutually consistent. Existing methods often trade off controllability and reliability: seed-based rewriting is flexible but weakly verifiable, whereas diagram-first construction improves validity but is less suited to arbitrary user-specified constraints. We introduce VeriGeo, a controllable geometry generation framework grounded in executable reasoning traces. Given user constraints such as target concepts and difficulty, an Author agent generates a problem and diagram, and a Solver agent produces a proof-aligned solution. Both agents use a shared action sequence that connects natural language, diagrams, geometric constraints, and proof steps into a verifiable representation. A three-stage pipeline checks numerical consistency, analytical realizability, and global consistency, using verification-guided reflection to repair recoverable failures and reject unrecoverable ones. Across five LLM backbones, raw generations frequently fail these checks, while VeriGeo repairs a substantial fraction of the invalid attempts. Supervised fine-tuning on 8.7k examples generated by VeriGeo achieves the best reported GeoQA performance among end-to-end multimodal LLM-based solvers, and obtains strong results on PGPS9K and MathVista-GPS, demonstrating the effectiveness of verified synthetic data for improving multimodal geometry reasoning.

AI.tldr: VeriGeo is a controllable geometry generation framework that uses executable reasoning traces and a three-stage verification pipeline to produce consistent problem-diagram-solution triples, achieving state-of-the-art GeoQA performance via supervised fine-tuning on 8.7k verified synthetic examples.
AI.motivation: Geometry problem generation is useful for AI-assisted education and multimodal reasoning, but existing methods trade off controllability and reliability—seed-based rewriting is flexible but weakly verifiable, while diagram-first construction improves validity but cannot handle arbitrary user-specified constraints.
AI.method: VeriGeo uses an Author agent to generate problems/diagrams and a Solver agent to produce proof-aligned solutions, both operating over a shared executable action sequence. A three-stage pipeline checks numerical consistency, analytical realizability, and global consistency, with verification-guided reflection to repair or reject invalid generations.
AI.result: Across five LLM backbones, raw generations frequently fail verification checks, but VeriGeo repairs a substantial fraction. Supervised fine-tuning on 8.7k VeriGeo-generated examples achieves the best reported GeoQA performance among end-to-end multimodal LLM solvers, plus strong results on PGPS9K and MathVista-GPS.
AI.conclusion: Verified synthetic data from VeriGeo effectively improves multimodal geometry reasoning, demonstrating the value of consistency-guaranteed generation pipelines for downstream model training.

title: Self-Improving VLA Policies: Selected Diffusion Noise for Spurious-Robust Action Smoothing
summary: Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies enable strong generalization in robotic manipulation, but remain sensitive to spurious visual correlations and noisy action generation, leading to brittle behavior under perturbations. We introduce Selected Diffusion Noise (SDN), a simple, training-free test-time method that improves both robustness and success rate by leveraging the diffusion noise space as a controllable degree of freedom. SDN dynamically samples noise vectors that are maximally separated from a reference set to mitigate reliance on spurious cues, while selecting candidates that yield more coherent action trajectories. This dual objective encourages stable behavior even under object-masked observations and reduces action jitter without modifying model parameters. We evaluate SDN on two simulation benchmarks (Google Robot, Widow-X) and two real-world robotic datasets across multiple VLA policies, including pi_0, Groot-N1.5, and Groot-N1.6. SDN consistently improves success rates by +8% in simulation and +10% in real-world settings, while producing smoother and more stable actions. Our results highlight that diffusion noise selection can serve as an effective and general mechanism for enhancing VLA policies at test time.

AI.tldr: SDN is a training-free test-time method that selects optimal diffusion noise vectors to improve robustness and success rate of VLA policies in robotic manipulation.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based VLA policies suffer from sensitivity to spurious visual correlations and noisy action generation, leading to brittle behavior under perturbations.
AI.method: SDN dynamically samples noise vectors maximally separated from a reference set to reduce reliance on spurious cues, while selecting candidates yielding more coherent action trajectories.
AI.result: +8% success rate improvement in simulation (Google Robot, Widow-X) and +10% in real-world settings across pi_0, Groot-N1.5, Groot-N1.6; smoother and more stable actions.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion noise selection at test time is an effective, general mechanism for enhancing VLA policy robustness without modifying model parameters.

title: When Should Agent Trust Be Conditional? Characterizing and Attacking Skill-Conditional Reputation in Agent Swarms
summary: Open platforms increasingly route tasks among heterogeneous LLM agents--differing in base model, scaffold, and tool stack--whose competence varies sharply by skill: an agent excellent at one skill may be useless at another. The standard reputation approach summarizes each agent by a single global trust score, but that scalar is the wrong object here, because routing every task to the globally most-trusted agent leaves the value of specialization unclaimed. We study skill-conditional trust R(i | k)--the trust to place in agent i for a task requiring skill k, rather than one score per agent--and pose three falsifiable questions: when is conditioning worth it, how much cross-skill evidence should be borrowed, and whether that borrowing is safe. A controlled phase-diagram analysis answers the first two: conditional trust wins only in a specific regime--high agent heterogeneity, sparse per-skill evidence, and correlated skills--and the coupling strength beta that buys this data efficiency is dual-use, because the same cross-skill borrowing is also a laundering channel. On a public benchmark of 14 genuinely heterogeneous AppWorld agents, real pools land inside the beneficial regime--a small but genuine gain, with the per-skill best agent genuinely changing across skills. We then show that an attacker with cheap evidence in one skill and none in a target skill hijacks the conditional router, driving routing regret from 0 to 0.94 on a pool our zero-cost Conditional Information Value Test (CIVT) rates GREEN--while the ungated trust verdict it contaminates reads -0.06 instead of the honest +0.19. A zero-evidence gate bounds the attack but does not eliminate it; we characterize the residual cost under an explicit budget. We do not claim Sybil-resistance--we quantify the trade-off.

AI.tldr: This paper studies skill-conditional trust (per-skill trust scores) for routing tasks among heterogeneous LLM agents, showing it only helps in a specific regime (high heterogeneity, sparse evidence, correlated skills), but is vulnerable to attackers who can launder cheap evidence across skills to hijack routing decisions.
AI.motivation: Standard single-score reputation systems fail to capture the specialization of heterogeneous LLM agents, leading to suboptimal routing that ignores skill-specific competence.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled phase-diagram analysis to identify the regime where conditional trust is beneficial, then empirically validate on 14 AppWorld agents. They propose the Conditional Information Value Test (CIVT) to detect attacks and characterize attack budgets.
AI.result: Conditional trust wins only with high agent heterogeneity, sparse per-skill evidence, and correlated skills. Real agent pools lie in the beneficial regime with small gains. Attackers can hijack the router (regret 0→0.94) by injecting cheap evidence in one skill; the CIVT detects this even when trust scores appear benign.
AI.conclusion: Skill-conditional trust improves routing in specific conditions but introduces vulnerability to cross-skill evidence laundering; the trade-off between data efficiency and attack surface is fundamental and not eliminable, only quantifiable.

title: A Modular Dual-Arm Apple Harvesting Robot with Enhanced Field Performance
summary: Robotic apple harvesting offers a promising solution to labor shortages in commercial orchards, but low throughput and poor performance in orchard environments hinder its commercial adoption. This paper presents a modular dual-arm apple harvesting robot that uses a vertically stacked arms to enable simultaneous operation in the upper and lower zones of a single tree, simplifying platform positioning from multi-tree lateral repositioning to single-tree stops. Compared to our prior horizontal dual-arm system, the platform integrates 5 advances: (1)a foundation-model-based perception pipeline combining Grounding-DINO and EfficientViT-SAM for robust fruit localization in unstructured outdoor environments; (2)7th-order jerk-bounded trajectory generation paired with a Control Barrier Function safety filter to achieve fast yet safe arm motions; (3)a linear sweep harvesting strategy with a 10cm approach buffer and rotational detachment that improves picking reliability; (4)a temporal-logic-based dual-arm coordination policy with vision-arm async scheduling that maximizes usage of a shared vacuum source; and (5)field validation in 2 commercial orchards covering different apple varieties and tree architectures during the 2025 harvest season. Across the 1738 arm cycles collected in these field trials, the system achieved an 80.0% per-attempt success rate and a mean per-arm cycle time of 7.53s. Fruit damage assessments confirmed that 91.2% of robotically harvested fruit retained the highest USDA grade (Extra Fancy), with bruise rates between 2.4% and 4.9%. With further improvements in the picking cycle time and handling of heavy foliage occlusions, this new modular robot design holds promise for commercial harvesting of apples.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular dual-arm apple harvesting robot with vertically stacked arms, integrating five key advances including foundation-model-based perception, jerk-bounded trajectory generation, linear sweep harvesting strategy, temporal-logic-based coordination, and field validation across 2 commercial orchards, achieving 80.0% success rate, mean 7.53s cycle time, and 91.2% USDA Extra Fancy grade fruit.
AI.motivation: Robotic apple harvesting suffers from low throughput and poor performance in orchard environments, hindering commercial adoption. The work aims to address these challenges by improving system efficiency and reliability through a modular dual-arm design and integrated advances.
AI.method: The system uses vertically stacked arms for simultaneous operation in upper/lower tree zones with single-tree stops, and integrates five advances: (1) Grounding-DINO + EfficientViT-SAM perception, (2) 7th-order jerk-bounded trajectory with CBF safety filter, (3) linear sweep harvesting with 10cm buffer and rotational detachment, (4) temporal-logic-based dual-arm coordination with vision-arm async scheduling, (5) field validation in 2 commercial orchards across varieties and architectures.
AI.result: Across 1738 arm cycles: 80.0% per-attempt success rate, 7.53s mean per-arm cycle time, 91.2% USDA Extra Fancy grade fruit with bruise rates 2.4%-4.9%.
AI.conclusion: With further improvements in cycle time and handling of heavy foliage occlusions, the modular dual-arm robot design shows promise for commercial apple harvesting.

title: Closing the Reflection Gap: A Free Calibration Bonus for Agentic RL
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external environments and observe feedback such as execution results, error messages, and tool outputs. A well-functioning agent should be able to leverage this feedback to accurately assess its own performance. Yet we find a persistent reflection gap: LLM agents tend to mis-assess their own outputs after observing concrete environment feedback -- even for questions they correctly answered -- and standard RL barely helps due to a credit-assignment mismatch. To close this gap, we propose RefGRPO, a simple yet effective fix that augments standard RL algorithms with two key ingredients: a free calibration bonus computed by contrasting the agent's own reflection with the actual outcome (requiring no additional reward model, LLM judge, or external annotation), and a dynamic schedule on its coefficient. Compared to standard RL baselines, our method simultaneously improves reflection calibration (e.g., reduces underconfidence rate $44.4\% \to 7.7\%$) and task accuracy (e.g., $75.1\% \to 76.5\%$) on text-to-SQL across five benchmarks. The resulting calibrated reflection turns the agent into its own verifier grounded in environment feedback, which further enables (i) better self-improvement that uses reflections as pseudo-rewards without outcome supervision, and (ii) more effective test-time selective prediction by committing only to rollouts flagged as correct.

AI.tldr: LLM agents mis-assess their own outputs after observing environment feedback (reflection gap), which standard RL fails to fix due to credit-assignment mismatch. RefGRPO closes this gap by augmenting RL with a calibration bonus (contrasting reflection vs. actual outcome) and a dynamic schedule, improving both reflection calibration (underconfidence 44.4%→7.7%) and task accuracy (75.1%→76.5%) on text-to-SQL, enabling better self-improvement and selective prediction.
AI.motivation: LLM agents exhibit a persistent reflection gap: they mis-assess their own performance after observing environment feedback, even for correctly answered questions. Standard RL barely helps due to credit-assignment mismatch.
AI.method: RefGRPO augments standard RL with two components: (1) a free calibration bonus computed by contrasting the agent's own reflection with the actual outcome (no extra reward model, LLM judge, or annotation), and (2) a dynamic schedule on the bonus coefficient.
AI.result: Reduces underconfidence rate from 44.4% to 7.7% and improves task accuracy from 75.1% to 76.5% on text-to-SQL across five benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The calibrated reflection enables the agent to serve as its own verifier grounded in environment feedback, enabling better self-improvement via pseudo-rewards and more effective test-time selective prediction.

title: GAIT: Legged Robot Proprioceptive State Estimation with Attention over Inertial-Leg Tokens
summary: In this paper, we propose a method that applies Inertial-Leg (IL) tokenization to an attention-based network for proprioceptive state estimation in legged robots. Unlike existing learning-based state estimators that concatenate all sensor measurements into a single flat vector, the proposed architecture represents inertial measurements and leg-wise measurements as individual tokens and uses an attention mechanism to learn the relative importance of each measurement.This design allows the network to reweight each measurement according to the current contact condition, reflecting the fact that the reliability of forward kinematic measurements depends on whether the corresponding foot is in contact. Unlike conventional contact-aided estimators, however, the proposed method learns this behavior without relying on an explicit contact estimator or on explicit measurement updates based on a stationary contact assumption. To validate the proposed method, we conducted experiments on a Unitree Go1 robot, including debris terrain not modeled in simulation and gait patterns not seen during training. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves better estimation performance than existing learning-based state estimators under unseen gait patterns and also improves performance over contact-aided model-based methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes Inertial-Leg (IL) tokenization with attention mechanism for proprioceptive state estimation in legged robots, treating sensor measurements as individual tokens to learn reliability weighting without explicit contact estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based state estimators concatenate all sensor measurements into a flat vector and fail to capture the varying reliability of leg kinematic measurements based on foot contact conditions; explicit contact-aided estimators require separate contact detection and rely on stationary contact assumptions.
AI.method: IL tokenization represents inertial and leg-wise measurements as individual tokens, uses an attention mechanism to learn relative importance of each measurement reweighted by contact condition, without explicit contact estimator or stationary contact constraints.
AI.result: Experiments on Unitree Go1 robot on debris terrain and unseen gait patterns show better estimation performance than existing learning-based state estimators and improved performance over contact-aided model-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The attention-based tokenization approach effectively handles varying measurement reliability under different contact conditions and generalizes to unseen scenarios without explicit contact modeling.

title: SkillAudit: Ground-Truth-Free Skill Evolution via Paired Trajectory Auditing
summary: Agent skills are structured procedural packages that guide frozen LLM agents in specialized workflows. Skills rarely remain sufficient after deployment: edge cases, API changes, and deployment constraints become visible only through use, making skill evolution a practical necessity. Existing methods depend on privileged feedback such as held-out validation scores, hidden test outcomes, or environment rewards -- signals often unavailable when a practitioner has only a task description and workspace data. We introduce SkillAudit, a framework for evolving agent skills without ground-truth feedback. The key idea is paired trajectory auditing: at each iteration, the same task is executed with and without the candidate skill, isolating how the skill changes agent behavior without external labels. To turn behavioral differences into edit guidance, SkillAudit uses Process-Aligned Contrastive Evaluation (PACE), a cluster of evaluators that maps trajectory divergences to diagnostic signals linked to specific passages in the skill document. A structural verifier, compiled once from the task specification and then fixed, checks task constraints and rolls back harmful updates. SkillAudit routes edits through two pipelines: Refine removes noisy or irrelevant guidance from broadly useful skills, while Repair replaces passages that conflict with the task. Across 89 containerized tasks spanning 8 professional domains, SkillAudit achieves 73.9% average task reward, outperforming an agent without skills (40.9%) and the static expert skill (56.7%). These gains are obtained without accessing hidden tests, reference solutions, or external scoring functions during evolution.

AI.tldr: SkillAudit is a framework for evolving LLM agent skills without ground-truth feedback by using paired trajectory auditing and contrastive evaluation, achieving 73.9% average task reward across 89 containerized tasks, outperforming both skill-free agents (40.9%) and static expert skills (56.7%).
AI.motivation: Agent skills degrade after deployment due to edge cases, API changes, and deployment constraints. Existing skill evolution methods require privileged feedback (validation scores, test outcomes, environment rewards) that is often unavailable when practitioners only have a task description and workspace data.
AI.method: SkillAudit uses paired trajectory auditing (executing tasks with and without the candidate skill to isolate behavioral differences), Process-Aligned Contrastive Evaluation (PACE) to map trajectory divergences to diagnostic signals linked to specific skill passages, and a structural verifier for constraint checking. Edits are routed through two pipelines: Refine (removing noisy/irrelevant guidance) and Repair (replacing conflicting passages).
AI.result: Across 89 containerized tasks in 8 domains, SkillAudit achieves 73.9% average task reward vs. 40.9% for skill-free agents and 56.7% for static expert skills, all without accessing hidden tests, reference solutions, or external scoring functions.
AI.conclusion: SkillAudit demonstrates that effective skill evolution is possible without ground-truth feedback, using only task descriptions and workspace data, significantly outperforming both no-skill and static-skill baselines.

title: Robustness without Wrinkles: Parallel Simulation and Robust MPC for Certified Deformable Manipulation
summary: We present CORD-SLS, a real-time control method for safe deformable object manipulation, with a focus on ropes and cloth. At its core is a GPU-parallel differentiable simulator with contact smoothing which enables efficient gradient-based planning through intermittent contact. To robustly satisfy constraints under model and sensing uncertainty, we develop a real-time, GPU-parallel output-feedback robust model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that plans with this simulator. We further show that the simulator accelerates model-based RL for training neural manipulation policies. To improve real-world robustness, we use conformal prediction to calibrate visual-feedback and perception-error bounds for MPC, producing reachable tubes that enable high-probability safe control. We evaluate CORD-SLS on high-dimensional, contact-rich rope and cloth manipulation tasks in simulation and hardware, including obstacle avoidance, routing, folding, and smoothing. Across settings, CORD-SLS achieves millisecond-speed planning, exceeding baselines in safety, speed, and task success.

AI.tldr: CORD-SLS is a real-time control method for safe deformable object manipulation (ropes/cloth) using GPU-parallel differentiable simulation, output-feedback robust MPC, conformal prediction for safety guarantees, and model-based RL acceleration.
AI.motivation: Safe and fast manipulation of deformable objects (ropes, cloth) under model and sensing uncertainty remains challenging due to high dimensionality, contact-rich dynamics, and real-time constraints.
AI.method: GPU-parallel differentiable simulator with contact smoothing for gradient-based planning; real-time output-feedback robust MPC using this simulator; conformal prediction to calibrate visual-feedback and perception-error bounds for reachable tubes enabling high-probability safe control; simulator also accelerates model-based RL for policy training.
AI.result: Achieves millisecond-speed planning on high-dimensional rope and cloth tasks (obstacle avoidance, routing, folding, smoothing); exceeds baselines in safety, speed, and task success in both simulation and hardware.
AI.conclusion: GPU-parallel differentiable simulation combined with robust MPC and conformal prediction enables real-time, safe deformable object manipulation under uncertainty.

title: AFFORDANCE20Q: Evaluating Affordance Reasoning from Physical Properties
summary: Affordance reasoning, the inference of an object's action possibilities from its physical properties (e.g., shape and material), is fundamental to human physical understanding and increasingly critical for Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing affordance benchmarks largely expose explicit object identities in the evaluation setup, allowing models to rely on memorized object-affordance mappings rather than reasoning over physical properties. To address this gap, we introduce Affordance20Q, a novel affordance reasoning benchmark formulated as a 20-Questions game without exposing the object's identity. In each game, the model identifies a hidden object's affordance from a candidate set by asking yes/no questions about its physical properties. Affordance20Q comprises 1,009 games over 454 objects and 59 affordances, all manually filtered, refined, and annotated. We conduct comprehensive experiments with 15 state-of-the-art LLMs and find a substantial gap (~20 points) compared to human performance. A KL-based information-gain (IG) analysis further shows that models fail to ask discriminating questions as the game progresses. To close the gap, we develop KB-Anchored Rule Induction (KARI), a pipeline based on LLMs that generates affordance rules grounded in evidence from knowledge bases (KBs). KARI improves open-source LLMs by up to 15.2 points, while the limited coverage of KBs hinders further gains. We release all our code and data at https://github.com/1171-jpg/Affordance20Q.git

AI.tldr: Affordance20Q is a benchmark that tests LLMs on affordance reasoning (inferring action possibilities from physical properties) using a 20-Questions game format that hides object identity, revealing a ~20 point gap between LLMs and humans, with the KARI method improving open-source LLMs by up to 15.2 points.
AI.motivation: Existing affordance benchmarks expose explicit object identities, allowing LLMs to rely on memorized object-affordance mappings rather than reasoning over physical properties (shape, material). The authors aim to create a benchmark that truly tests physical property-based reasoning.
AI.method: The authors introduce Affordance20Q, a benchmark formatted as a 20-Questions game where the model identifies a hidden object's affordance from a candidate set by asking yes/no questions about physical properties, without revealing the object's identity. It includes 1,009 games over 454 objects and 59 affordances. They also develop KARI (KB-Anchored Rule Induction), a pipeline that generates affordance rules grounded in evidence from knowledge bases.
AI.result: Experiments with 15 state-of-the-art LLMs show a substantial ~20 point gap compared to human performance. KL-based information-gain analysis reveals models fail to ask discriminating questions as the game progresses. KARI improves open-source LLMs by up to 15.2 points, though limited KB coverage hinders further gains.
AI.conclusion: LLMs significantly underperform humans on genuine affordance reasoning when object identity is hidden. The KARI method demonstrates that grounding in knowledge bases can partially close this gap, but the limited coverage of KBs remains a bottleneck for further improvement.

authors: Lars A. T. H. van Alen
René M. J. G. van de Molengraft
title: Short-Horizon Position Accuracy of Single-Track Models: Implications for Motion Planning of Autonomous Vehicles
comment: Submitted to The International Journal of Automotive Engineering, Official Journal of the Society of Automotive Engineers of Japan, Inc. (JSAE)
summary: Accurate and computationally efficient vehicle models are essential for motion planning of autonomous vehicles, where positional accuracy directly affects trajectory feasibility and safety. However, the positional accuracy has not been systematically evaluated against real measurements. Therefore, this paper compares the short-horizon positional accuracy of three single-track vehicle models against vehicle measurements across various driving maneuvers. Model parameters are identified through dedicated experiments with the instrumented test vehicle. Rather than identifying a single best model, this work aims to provide insight into the trade-offs between model complexity, parameterization quality, and positional accuracy for informed model selection in Model Predictive Control applications.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the short-horizon positional accuracy of three single-track vehicle models against real measurements to understand trade-offs between model complexity, parameterization quality, and positional accuracy for MPC applications.
AI.motivation: Accurate vehicle models are critical for motion planning safety, but positional accuracy against real measurements has not been systematically evaluated, leaving a gap in informed model selection.
AI.method: Three single-track vehicle models were compared against instrumented test vehicle measurements across various maneuvers; model parameters were identified through dedicated experiments to assess positional accuracy.
AI.result: The study provides quantitative comparisons of positional accuracy across models and maneuvers, revealing trade-offs rather than a single best model.
AI.conclusion: Trade-offs between model complexity, parameterization quality, and positional accuracy should guide model selection for MPC, rather than assuming one model universally outperforms others.

title: HarnessX: A Composable, Adaptive, and Evolvable Agent Harness Foundry
summary: AI agent performance depends critically on the runtime harness, comprising the prompts, tools, memory, and control flow that mediate how a model observes, reasons, and acts. Yet today's harnesses remain largely hand-crafted and static: each new model or task still demands bespoke scaffolding, and the rich traces produced during execution are rarely distilled back into systematic improvement. We introduce HarnessX, a foundry for composable, adaptive, and evolvable agent harnesses. HarnessX assembles typed harness primitives via a substitution algebra, adapts them through AEGIS, a trace-driven multi-agent evolution engine grounded in an operational mirror between symbolic adaptation and reinforcement learning, and closes the harness-model loop by turning trajectories into both harness updates and model training signal. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop, tau^3-Bench, and SWE-bench Verified), HarnessX yields an average gain of +14.5% (up to +44.0%), with gains largest where baselines are lowest. These results suggest that agent progress need not come from model scaling alone: composing and evolving runtime interfaces from execution feedback is an actionable and complementary lever. The complete codebase will be open-sourced in a future release.

AI.tldr: HarnessX is a composable, adaptive, and evolvable framework for building AI agent runtime harnesses (prompts, tools, memory, control flow). It uses a substitution algebra for assembly, AEGIS for trace-driven multi-agent evolution, and closes the harness-model loop by leveraging execution trajectories for both harness updates and model training. Across five benchmarks, it achieves an average +14.5% gain (up to +44.0%), demonstrating that evolving runtime interfaces from execution feedback is a complementary lever to model scaling.
AI.motivation: Current agent harnesses are hand-crafted and static; each new model or task requires bespoke scaffolding, and execution traces are not systematically used for improvement.
AI.method: HarnessX uses (1) typed harness primitives assembled via a substitution algebra, (2) AEGIS, a trace-driven multi-agent evolution engine with an operational mirror linking symbolic adaptation and reinforcement learning, and (3) a closed loop where trajectories inform both harness updates and model training signal.
AI.result: Average gain of +14.5% (up to +44.0%) across ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop, tau^3-Bench, and SWE-bench Verified, with largest gains where baselines were lowest.
AI.conclusion: Agent progress does not require model scaling alone; composing and evolving runtime interfaces from execution feedback is an actionable and complementary lever for improvement.

title: Universal Manipulation Exoskeleton: Learning Compliant Whole-body Policies with Real-time Torque Feedback
summary: For robots to work safely in household environments, they need to be compliant and react to torque and force feedback during contact. However, the majority of existing data collection pipelines still lack the ability to capture force and torque data for learning active compliant policies. In this paper, we present Universal Manipulation Exoskeleton (UME), an upper-limb exoskeleton that provides real-time haptic torque feedback while recording whole-arm configurations and joint torque signals for teleoperation. With transparent torque feedback, human operators can even unsheathe kinematically constrained objects while blindfolded. UME is low-cost, lightweight, and portable. Equipped with an embedded IMU, it enables teleoperation for mobile manipulation. With our proposed universal retargeting algorithm, UME can teleoperate a range of robots, including the 7DoF OpenArm, 7DoF Franka, and 6DoF X-ARM. We demonstrate that this combination of capabilities enables learning bimanual, whole-body, and active compliant policies that operate effectively in highly constrained spaces. The learned robust autonomous policies achieve high success rates across a variety of tasks, including long-horizon mobile manipulation, force-mediated box flipping, visually occluded box pushing, and space-constrained tabletop manipulation. Videos, code, and additional information can be found at https://ume-exo.github.io.

AI.tldr: UME is a low-cost, lightweight upper-limb exoskeleton that provides real-time haptic torque feedback and records whole-arm configurations and joint torque signals for teleoperation, enabling learning of bimanual, whole-body, and active compliant policies for safe robot manipulation in household environments.
AI.motivation: Existing data collection pipelines lack the ability to capture force and torque data needed for learning active compliant policies, which are essential for robots to work safely in household environments.
AI.method: The authors present UME, an upper-limb exoskeleton with real-time haptic torque feedback, embedded IMU for mobile teleoperation, and a universal retargeting algorithm compatible with multiple robot arms (7DoF OpenArm, 7DoF Franka, 6DoF X-ARM).
AI.result: UME enables teleoperation with transparent torque feedback (unsheathing kinematically constrained objects blindfolded), and the learned policies achieve high success rates in tasks including long-horizon mobile manipulation, force-mediated box flipping, visually occluded box pushing, and space-constrained tabletop manipulation.
AI.conclusion: The combination of haptic torque feedback, universal retargeting, and portability enables learning robust autonomous compliant policies that operate effectively in highly constrained spaces for bimanual and whole-body manipulation.

title: Communication Policy Evolution for Proactive LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents have rapidly evolved into autonomous systems, yet a persistent information gap remains between users and agents: communication is costly, while users' identical preferences further limit information exchange. To investigate how agents should communicate across modalities, this paper formalizes Communication Policy, establishes textual and UI-based policies, and then evaluates communication policies across diverse environments, personas, and model combinations. Building information asymmetry for proactive agents, we set up two complementary settings, User-Agent and Planner-Executor. Experimental results reveal complementary strengths between interaction channels: text-based interaction often facilitates task performance, while structured UI improves agents' response quality and persona compliance. Motivated by that, a hybrid method combines these advantages. We further propose Communication Policy Evolution (CPE), a self-evolution framework for refining communication policies through rollout and prompt-level evolving. Without model modification, CPE achieves the best task success across multiple settings using prompt refinement alone. Our findings identify communication behavior as a critical yet underexplored design dimension for LLM agents.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes Communication Policy for LLM agents, evaluates text vs. UI communication modalities, finds complementary strengths (text improves task performance, UI improves response quality and persona compliance), and proposes Communication Policy Evolution (CPE) that self-evolves policies via rollout and prompt-level refinement to achieve best task success without model modification.
AI.motivation: There is a persistent information gap between users and LLM agents due to costly communication and identical user preferences limiting information exchange. The authors aim to investigate how agents should communicate across different modalities to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The paper formalizes Communication Policy, establishes textual and UI-based policies, and evaluates them across diverse environments, personas, and model combinations. Two settings are introduced: User-Agent and Planner-Executor. A hybrid method combining both modalities is proposed, along with Communication Policy Evolution (CPE), a self-evolution framework using rollout and prompt-level evolving.
AI.result: Text-based interaction facilitates task performance, while structured UI improves response quality and persona compliance. The hybrid method combines these advantages. CPE achieves the best task success across multiple settings through prompt refinement alone, without model modification.
AI.conclusion: Communication behavior is a critical yet underexplored design dimension for LLM agents. CPE demonstrates that prompt-level self-evolution can effectively optimize communication policies without modifying the underlying model.

title: Selective Agentic Recovery for UAV Autonomy with a Persistent Mission Runtime
summary: Agentic AI can support unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) autonomy by providing high-level recovery reasoning when local waypoint- or setpoint-based execution encounters blocked passages, repeated no-progress behavior, or mission-level ambiguity. On physical UAVs, however, remote reasoning is most useful when it is invoked selectively, since each call introduces latency, resource cost, backend uncertainty, and a need to validate the returned decision. This paper presents Persistent Mission Runtime (PMR), a UAV recovery framework that keeps the mission loop and safety-critical execution local while using an external agentic reasoner only as an on-demand recovery module. The reasoner selects from predefined recovery skills, and each returned decision is parsed, verified, safety-filtered, and mapped to local executor actions before it can affect flight. PMR introduces learned Cognitive Value of Invocation (learned-CVI), a compact admission gate that estimates when remote agentic reasoning is likely to improve near-term mission progress enough to justify its operational cost. Across a fixed 400-run Gazebo/PX4 benchmark with eight scenarios, learned-CVI raises hard/ambiguous-regime success from 5.0% under local-only autonomy to 95.0%, outperforms one-shot and periodic reasoning baselines by 20.0 and 32.5 percentage points, and reduces remote-agent calls by 16.7% and logged tokens by 29.2% relative to a manually tuned rule-based invocation baseline.

AI.tldr: PMR is a UAV recovery framework that keeps mission execution local while using an external agentic AI reasoner only on-demand. A learned Cognitive Value of Invocation (learned-CVI) gate decides when to call the remote reasoner, improving success rates from 5% to 95% in ambiguous scenarios while reducing remote calls by 16.7% relative to rule-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI can support UAV autonomy via high-level recovery reasoning, but remote reasoning calls introduce latency, cost, uncertainty, and require validation. The challenge is to invoke the remote reasoner selectively to maximize benefit while minimizing operational overhead.
