AI.method: PMR keeps the mission loop and safety-critical execution local, using an external agentic reasoner only as an on-demand recovery module. The reasoner selects from predefined recovery skills; each decision is parsed, verified, safety-filtered, and mapped to local executor actions. A learned Cognitive Value of Invocation (learned-CVI) gate estimates when remote reasoning will improve near-term mission progress enough to justify its cost.
AI.result: In a 400-run Gazebo/PX4 benchmark with eight scenarios, learned-CVI raised hard/ambiguous-regime success from 5.0% (local-only) to 95.0%, outperformed one-shot and periodic reasoning baselines by 20.0 and 32.5 percentage points, and reduced remote-agent calls by 16.7% and logged tokens by 29.2% vs. a manually tuned rule-based invocation baseline.
AI.conclusion: PMR with learned-CVI provides an effective selective invocation mechanism for agentic AI in UAV recovery, achieving high success rates with reduced communication overhead compared to alternative invocation strategies.

title: CSPO: Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization for Safe Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted as a Spotlight paper at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Safe reinforcement learning (Safe RL) aims to maximize expected return while satisfying safety constraints, typically modeled as Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). While primal-dual methods scale well to deep RL, they often suffer from delayed constraint correction, leading to oscillatory behavior and prolonged safety violations. In this paper, we propose Constraint-Sensitive Policy Optimization (CSPO), a first-order primal-dual method that incorporates local constraint sensitivity into policy updates. CSPO augments the primal objective with a constraint-sensitive correction derived from the shortest signed distance to the safety boundary, enabling smarter recovery steps back to safety, compensating for delayed Lagrange multiplier updates, reducing oscillations near the boundary, and preserving the KKT solutions of the original constrained problem. Experiments on navigation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that CSPO achieves faster safety recovery and high reward preservation, resulting in higher constrained returns compared to state-of-the-art primal-dual and penalty-based methods

AI.tldr: CSPO is a first-order primal-dual method for Safe RL that incorporates local constraint sensitivity via shortest signed distance to the safety boundary, compensating for delayed Lagrange multiplier updates to achieve faster safety recovery and higher constrained returns.
AI.motivation: Primal-dual methods for Safe RL suffer from delayed constraint correction, causing oscillatory behavior and prolonged safety violations.
AI.method: CSPO augments the primal objective with a constraint-sensitive correction derived from the shortest signed distance to the safety boundary, enabling smarter recovery steps while preserving KKT solutions.
AI.result: Faster safety recovery and high reward preservation, achieving higher constrained returns than state-of-the-art primal-dual and penalty-based methods on navigation and locomotion benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating local constraint sensitivity into primal-dual updates effectively mitigates delayed multiplier correction, reducing oscillations and improving safety-reward trade-offs in Safe RL.

title: BIM-Loc: BIM-Integrated Discrepancy-Aware LiDAR-based Indoor Localization
comment: 24 pages, 21 figures, accepted by International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR), to be published
summary: Accurate and robust localization is a fundamental requirement for service and inspection robots, particularly in feature-sparse indoor environments where traditional systems struggle due to a lack of distinct landmarks. While prior maps can enhance robustness, precise and compact maps capturing real-world details are often unavailable for new or frequently changing environments. This paper presents BIM-Loc, a novel discrepancy-aware LiDAR-based localization method that directly integrates Building Information Models (BIM) from the design phase. BIM-Loc simultaneously estimates trajectories aligned with the BIM coordinate system and identifies discrepancies between real-world observations and the as-designed BIM in an online fashion. Our core contributions include: (1) a novel multi-hit ray casting strategy for efficient BIM-point data association and projection of 3D observations into 2D texture space; (2) a pose graph optimization framework with BIM-integrated factors that enforces consistency among odometry, sequential scans, and BIM structures; and (3) a hierarchical Bayesian inference module that incrementally updates a continuous 2D surface representation for discrepancy detection, propagating updates from the pixel to the structure level. Extensive evaluations in both simulation and real-world applications demonstrate that BIM-Loc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art map-based methods in localization accuracy and robustness.

AI.tldr: BIM-Loc is a LiDAR-based localization method that uses Building Information Models (BIM) from the design phase to achieve accurate and robust robot localization in feature-sparse indoor environments, while simultaneously detecting discrepancies between real-world observations and the as-designed BIM.
AI.motivation: Traditional localization systems struggle in feature-sparse indoor environments due to lack of distinct landmarks. Prior maps can enhance robustness but are often unavailable or outdated for new or frequently changing environments. The authors propose leveraging BIM from the design phase as a readily available prior.
AI.method: BIM-Loc introduces three key contributions: (1) a multi-hit ray casting strategy for efficient BIM-point data association and 3D-to-2D texture projection; (2) a pose graph optimization framework with BIM-integrated factors enforcing consistency among odometry, scans, and BIM structures; and (3) a hierarchical Bayesian inference module for incremental continuous 2D surface representation and discrepancy detection.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations in both simulation and real-world applications show BIM-Loc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art map-based methods in localization accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: BIM-Loc enables accurate and robust localization directly from design-phase BIM models without requiring pre-built prior maps, while also providing online discrepancy detection between as-designed and as-built environments.

title: Causal Object-Centric Models for Planning with Monte Carlo Tree Search
summary: We introduce COMET (Causal Object-centric Model for Efficient Tree search), a model-based reinforcement learning algorithm that performs Monte Carlo Tree Search in a slot-structured latent space. COMET pairs a frozen unsupervised object-centric encoder with a transformer-based world model, in which actions are bound to objects through a novel action-slot fusion mechanism that is used in slot transition prediction. Policy and value heads use object-causal attention, modulating token interactions by learned per-slot relevance scores so that decision-making concentrates on task-relevant entities. COMET adds an explicit object-level inductive bias to MuZero-style latent planning. Across eight visually and dynamically diverse tasks from the Object-Centric Visual RL benchmark, ManiSkill, Robosuite, and VizDoom, COMET achieves a higher mean normalized score during the early stages of training compared to object-centric and monolithic baselines.

AI.tldr: COMET is a model-based RL algorithm that performs Monte Carlo Tree Search in a slot-structured latent space, using an unsupervised object-centric encoder, transformer world model with action-slot fusion, and object-causal attention for decision-making, achieving superior early training performance across diverse visual RL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To improve sample efficiency and generalization in model-based reinforcement learning by incorporating explicit object-level inductive biases into latent planning (MuZero-style), enabling the agent to focus on task-relevant entities rather than processing monolithic scene representations.
AI.method: COMET combines a frozen unsupervised object-centric encoder with a transformer-based world model. Actions are bound to objects via a novel action-slot fusion mechanism for slot transition prediction. Policy and value heads employ object-causal attention with learned per-slot relevance scores to concentrate on task-relevant entities during Monte Carlo Tree Search in slot-structured latent space.
AI.result: Across eight visually and dynamically diverse tasks from Object-Centric Visual RL benchmark, ManiSkill, Robosuite, and VizDoom, COMET achieves higher mean normalized score during early training stages compared to both object-centric and monolithic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Adding explicit object-level inductive bias to latent planning improves early training performance in model-based RL, suggesting that structured object-centric representations benefit sample efficiency and task-relevant decision-making in complex visual environments.

title: When and How Severely: Scenario-Specific Safety Envelopes for Driving VLAs
summary: Safety certification of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) driving planners under ISO 21448 (SOTIF) rests on an Operational Design Domain (ODD) specification that answers two complementary questions: when does the planner start to fail, and how severely does it fail once it does? We evaluate Alpamayo R1, a 10B-parameter open-weight driving VLA, on 15,968 (clip, attack) pairs. We find a conservative-aggregate gap: an aggregate safe threshold of $σ\leq 50$ under a 15% average displacement error (ADE) budget masks well-sampled scenarios that tolerate the top of the tested grid ($σ= 70$). A Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) on the changed-explanation subset identifies six discrete severity bands (BIC-optimal $k{=}6$), so two perturbation conditions with the same mean error can differ materially in their share of high-severity (C4/C5) failures. Joining the two analyses on the same corpus surfaces a finding neither yields in isolation: the scenarios with the loosest noise thresholds are not those with the lowest high-severity rate: STOP_SIGNAL concentrates roughly $4\times$ the C4/C5 share of LANE_KEEPING despite tolerating a larger $σ$. A deployable SOTIF ODD specification for driving VLAs therefore requires a two-dimensional safety envelope, not a single aggregate value per hazard.

AI.tldr: Safety certification of VLA driving planners under ISO 21448 requires a two-dimensional ODD safety envelope (failure threshold + severity distribution), as demonstrated by analyzing Alpamayo R1 across 15,968 scenarios. A single aggregate threshold masks critical variation: e.g., STOP_SIGNAL tolerates higher noise but has ~4× more high-severity failures than LANE_KEEPING.
AI.motivation: ISO 21448 (SOTIF) safety certification of VLA driving planners requires an ODD specification that answers when the planner starts to fail and how severely it fails, but existing approaches rely on single aggregate thresholds that may obscure critical failure modes.
AI.method: Evaluated Alpamayo R1 (10B-parameter VLA) on 15,968 (clip, attack) pairs. Used conservative-aggregate gap analysis (σ ≤ 50 under 15% ADE budget) and Gaussian Mixture Model (BIC-optimal k=6) on changed-explanation subsets to identify severity bands.
AI.result: 1) Aggregate safe threshold σ≤50 masks well-sampled scenarios tolerating σ=70. 2) GMM identifies six discrete severity bands (C4/C5). 3) Two perturbation conditions with same mean error differ materially in high-severity share. 4) STOP_SIGNAL has ~4× higher C4/C5 share than LANE_KEEPING despite tolerating larger σ.
AI.conclusion: A deployable SOTIF ODD specification for driving VLAs requires a two-dimensional safety envelope (threshold + severity distribution), not a single aggregate value per hazard.

title: GitOfThoughts: Version-Controlled Reasoning and Agent Memory You Can Replay, Diff, and Merge
summary:
Large language model (LLM) reasoning is ephemeral: chains of thought vanish with the context window, pruned search branches leave no record, and memory buffers cannot be diffed, merged, or audited. Every other complex software process (code, infrastructure, data, experiments) is version-controlled; reasoning is not. We introduce GitOfThoughts, which stores an agent's reasoning tree as a git repository: every scored thought is a commit, scores are notes, outcomes are tags, and retrieval is "git log" over the agent's own history. This makes reasoning replayable, auditable, and mergeable across agents at near-zero engineering cost.
  We then ask the harder question: does memory, in any substrate, actually improve accuracy? Across five substrates (none, markdown, vector, graph, git), two benchmarks, two model scales, and pre-registered replications, the answer for novel problems is no. No memory format reliably helps, and a promising early result collapsed under its own pre-registered replication. Memory pays only above what we call the copyability threshold: when the retrieved case is a near-duplicate of the current problem (similarity >~ 0.8), accuracy jumps sharply; below it, nothing. The gain is answer retrieval, not method transfer: a 4.5x larger model doubles the near-duplicate payoff yet still cannot extract a transferable method from a worked example. The only general lever we find is test-time sampling. The case for git-as-substrate is therefore auditability, provenance, and mergeability at accuracy parity. We document a retracted result and a refuted hypothesis to model the evaluation standard we hold ourselves to.

AI.tldr: GitOfThoughts stores LLM reasoning trees as git repos for replayability, auditability, and merging. However, on novel problems, no memory substrate (including git) improves accuracy; only near-duplicate retrieval (similarity >0.8) helps, and the gain is answer copying, not method transfer. The only consistent accuracy lever is test-time sampling.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning is ephemeral and cannot be version-controlled like other software processes. The authors aim to address this gap by proposing a git-based substrate for reasoning, and then critically investigate whether memory in any form actually improves accuracy on novel problems.
AI.method: GitOfThoughts stores each scored thought as a commit, scores as notes, outcomes as tags, and uses "git log" for retrieval. The authors then systematically evaluate five memory substrates (none, markdown, vector, graph, git) across two benchmarks, two model scales, and pre-registered replications to test whether memory improves accuracy.
AI.result: No memory format reliably improves accuracy on novel problems. A promising early result collapsed under pre-registered replication. Accuracy improves only above the "copyability threshold" (similarity > ~0.8, near-duplicate retrieval). The gain is answer copying, not method transfer—even a 4.5x larger model cannot extract a transferable method. The only general lever is test-time sampling.
AI.conclusion: The case for git-as-substrate is auditability, provenance, and mergeability at accuracy parity, not accuracy gains. Memory is not a general solution for novel reasoning problems; only near-duplicate retrieval and test-time sampling help.

title: SyLink Hand: A Synergy-Inspired Linkage-Driven Anthropomorphic Hand for Human-Like Dexterity
summary: Designing anthropomorphic robotic hands that balance functional dexterity with mechanical simplicity remains a significant challenge. Inspired by human hand synergies, this paper presents the SyLink Hand, an anthropomorphic dexterous hand that integrates biomechanical synergy principles with linkage-driven transmission mechanisms to achieve a high degree of anthropomorphism in appearance, kinematics, and functionality within a compact and cost-effective architecture. Biomechanical analysis of natural hand motions using motion capture gloves reveals strong kinematic correlations among hand joints, providing the basis for a simplified yet functional degree-of-freedom (DOF) configuration. Guided by these synergistic characteristics, optimized linkage mechanisms are employed to coordinate multiple joint motions and reproduce natural finger trajectories. A novel spherical four-bar linkage is further proposed to achieve decoupled flexion/extension (Flex/Ext) and abduction/adduction (Abd/Add) at the metacarpophalangeal joint within a compact form factor. The resulting prototype integrates 19 joints driven by 11 actuators, with a total mass of 520g and a manufacturing cost of approximately USD 400. Experimental evaluations demonstrate its human-like kinematic performance, high load-bearing capability, and versatile grasping and manipulation skills. These results validate that the synergy-inspired, linkage-based design effectively balances anthropomorphism, mechanical simplicity, and functional versatility, highlighting its potential for practical deployment in dexterity-demanding robotic applications.

AI.tldr: The SyLink Hand is an anthropomorphic robotic hand that uses biomechanical synergy principles and linkage-driven mechanisms to achieve human-like dexterity, kinematics, and grasping capabilities with only 11 actuators driving 19 joints, costing ~$400 and weighing 520g.
AI.motivation: Designing anthropomorphic robotic hands that balance functional dexterity with mechanical simplicity remains a significant challenge; this work aims to achieve high anthropomorphism in appearance, kinematics, and functionality within a compact and cost-effective architecture.
AI.method: Biomechanical analysis of natural hand motions via motion capture gloves reveals kinematic synergies; optimized linkage mechanisms coordinate multiple joint motions; a novel spherical four-bar linkage achieves decoupled Flex/Ext and Abd/Add at the MCP joint in a compact form.
AI.result: 19 joints driven by 11 actuators, 520g mass, ~$400 cost; human-like kinematic performance, high load-bearing capability, versatile grasping and manipulation skills demonstrated experimentally.
AI.conclusion: The synergy-inspired, linkage-based design effectively balances anthropomorphism, mechanical simplicity, and functional versatility, showing potential for practical deployment in dexterity-demanding robotic applications.

title: When the Tool Decides: LLM Agents Defer Blindly to Graph Neural Network Tools, and Stronger Backbones Defer More
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Under review at TMLR
summary: A growing line of work equips large language model (LLM) agents with graph neural networks (GNNs) as callable tools, assuming the agent exercises judgment over when and how much to rely on such a tool. We test this directly. We expose a frozen GNN to a ReAct-style LLM agent as an explicit tool and measure, on node classification over a text-attributed graph (ogbn-arxiv, replicated on WikiCS), whether the agent uses the tool or merely obeys it. We find the agent does not exercise judgment: its predictions agree with the raw GNN's 97.6-99.2% of the time (5 seeds), collapsing into a GNN parrot that adopts the tool's output wholesale and bypasses its own reasoning. Sweeping backbone capability (Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B), the deference is not a weak-model artifact: among models able to invoke the tool, agreement rises with capability (0.60 to 0.98 from 1.5B to 7B). Crucially, the cost of deference does not shrink as capability grows and grows where alternatives emerge: a per-node oracle over the available actions beats the parrot by 0.09-0.18 at 3B and 0.12-0.22 at 7B, roughly doubling at high homophily, because the parrot is pinned to the frozen GNN while the agent's alternatives improve; at 7B a simple neighbour-label tool overtakes the GNN at high homophily (0.81 vs 0.71) yet the agent still defers. A simple selective-invocation gate recovers about half of that high-homophily gap (0.71 to 0.83) but yields no net global gain, and held-out estimates bound the best achievable gate over standard test-time features to at most a third of the oracle headroom: reliable selective invocation looks limited by available information, not merely router design. Our results are a cautionary measurement: evaluations of agent+tool systems cannot assume the agent adds judgment on top of the tool, and selective invocation must be designed in rather than expected to emerge from scale.

AI.tldr: LLM agents equipped with GNN tools do not exercise judgment but instead act as "GNN parrots," deferring to the tool's output 97.6-99.2% of the time. This deference increases with model capability, and the performance gap widens when better alternatives exist. Selective invocation gates recover only half the gap, with information limitations constraining further improvement.
AI.motivation: To test whether LLM agents equipped with GNN tools actually exercise judgment over when and how much to rely on the tool, or merely obey it wholesale without reasoning.
AI.method: Exposed a frozen GNN as a callable tool to a ReAct-style LLM agent on node classification tasks (ogbn-arxiv, WikiCS); measured agreement rates between agent and raw GNN outputs; swept backbone capability from 0.5B to 7B parameters; compared against oracle and selective-invocation gate baselines.
AI.result: Agreement between agent and GNN is 97.6-99.2% (5 seeds). Deference increases with model capability (0.60 to 0.98 from 1.5B to 7B). Oracle outperforms parrot by 0.09-0.18 at 3B and 0.12-0.22 at 7B, doubling at high homophily. A selective-invocation gate recovers ~50% of the high-homophily gap but yields no net global gain. Held-out estimates bound achievable gate improvement to at most 1/3 of oracle headroom.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of agent+tool systems cannot assume agents add judgment on top of tools; selective invocation must be explicitly designed rather than expected to emerge from scale. Available information, not just router design, fundamentally limits reliable selective invocation.

title: Optimality-Preserving Decomposition for Scalable QAOA in Natural-Language-Guided Multi-Drone Assignment
summary: As multi-drone fleets scale, zone assignment rapidly evolves into an intractable NP-hard combinatorial problem that overwhelms classical exhaustive search. While quantum optimization promises to shatter these classical bottlenecks, mapping complex spatial tasks from human intent to restricted quantum hardware remains a severe challenge. To bridge this gap, we present an end-to-end framework integrating a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM) front-end with a highly scalable, domain-specific quantum-classical backend. The front-end utilizes Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to translate free-form natural language instructions into structurally robust Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) constraints without false negatives. To overcome the strict qubit limits of near-term quantum devices, our framework features a novel constraint-preserving graph partitioner and a compressed separator-based dynamic programming (DP) merge. By structurally encoding constraints via W-state initialization and XY-mixers in Conditional Value-at-Risk Quantum Approximate Optimization (CVaR-QAOA), the pipeline stays highly compact. Empirical results demonstrate that this architecture circumvents classical scaling walls, recovering the global optimum on 100% of idealized oracle cases and 96.3% under real QAOA sampling, enabling natural-language-guided task allocation at previously intractable scales.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end framework integrating an LLM front-end (SFT+DPO fine-tuned) with a quantum-classical backend (CVaR-QAOA, constraint-preserving graph partitioner, DP merge) to translate natural language into QUBO constraints for multi-drone zone assignment, achieving 100% optimum on idealized cases and 96.3% under real QAOA sampling.
AI.motivation: Multi-drone zone assignment is an NP-hard combinatorial problem unsolvable by classical exhaustive search at scale; quantum optimization offers potential but mapping human intent to quantum hardware constraints is a severe bottleneck.
AI.method: LLM front-end: SFT + DPO fine-tuning to translate natural language into QUBO constraints. Backend: constraint-preserving graph partitioner, separator-based DP merge for qubit reduction, CVaR-QAOA with W-state initialization and XY-mixers.
AI.result: 100% global optimum recovery on idealized oracle cases, 96.3% under real QAOA sampling; bypasses classical scaling walls at previously intractable scales.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LLM-to-quantum pipeline enables natural-language-guided task allocation for multi-drone fleets at scales beyond classical reach, effectively bridging human intent and quantum hardware limitations.

title: From Chatbot to Digital Colleague: The Paradigm Shift Toward Persistent Autonomous AI
comment: The paper is available on the project website: https://from-chatbot-to-digital-colleague.github.io/
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are undergoing a fundamental transformation from conversational generators into integrated AI systems capable of reasoning, action, memory, and self-improvement. We conceptualize this transition as a shift from Chatbot to Digital Colleague: from conversational answers to persistent work. We organize this transition along two tightly coupled dimensions. First, at the cognitive core level, LLMs are advancing from Chatbot-era "fast thinking" systems driven by next-token prediction toward Thinking LLMs that leverage inference-time computation, Chain-of-Thought reasoning, reflection, process supervision, and reinforcement learning to support more deliberate and reliable cognition. Second, at the tool-augmented task execution level, LLMs are progressing from tool-calling Agents that invoke external resources in an ad hoc manner toward OpenClaw-style workstation systems (OpenClaw) equipped with persistent Workspaces, skills, verification loops, and governance. The "Workspace + Skill" paradigm makes episodic tool use colleague-like via state persistence, reusable procedures, task closure, and experience reuse. We examine data construction shifts from instruction-response pairs to State-Action-Observation trajectories and evaluation from static benchmarks to sandboxed, auditable, self-evolving AI ecosystems.

AI.tldr: This paper conceptualizes the evolution of LLMs from conversational Chatbots to persistent Digital Colleagues, spanning two dimensions: (1) cognitive advancement from fast-thinking next-token prediction to deliberate Thinking LLMs with Chain-of-Thought, reflection, and reinforcement learning, and (2) tool-augmented execution from ad hoc Agents to OpenClaw-style workstation systems with persistent Workspaces, skills, verification loops, and governance, supported by shifts in data construction (instruction-response pairs to State-Action-Observation trajectories) and evaluation (static benchmarks to sandboxed, self-evolving ecosystems).
AI.motivation: To conceptualize and formalize the ongoing paradigm shift of LLMs from conversational generators to integrated, persistent AI systems capable of reasoning, action, memory, and self-improvement.
AI.method: Organizes the transition along two tightly coupled dimensions: (1) the cognitive core level examining the shift from fast-thinking next-token prediction to Thinking LLMs with inference-time computation, Chain-of-Thought, reflection, process supervision, and RL; (2) the tool-augmented task execution level examining the progression from ad hoc tool-calling Agents to OpenClaw-style workstation systems with persistent Workspaces, skills, verification loops, and governance. Analyzes corresponding shifts in data construction and evaluation paradigms.
AI.result: Identifies a dual-dimensional transition: cognitive core evolves from fast thinking to deliberate reasoning; tool execution evolves from episodic agents to persistent workstation systems with Workspace+Skill paradigm enabling state persistence, reusable procedures, task closure, and experience reuse. Data shifts from instruction-response pairs to State-Action-Observation trajectories; evaluation shifts from static benchmarks to sandboxed, auditable, self-evolving ecosystems.
AI.conclusion: The LLM field is undergoing a fundamental transformation from Chatbot to Digital Colleague, requiring new paradigms in cognition, tool use, data construction, and evaluation to support persistent, reliable, and self-improving AI systems.

title: ReactVLA: Fast and Lightweight Reactive Robot Manipulation via Improved Mean Flow Action Generation
summary: Diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong capability in modeling expressive and multimodal action distributions. However, their reliance on iterative sampling introduces substantial inference latency, which limits their applicability to reactive closed-loop robot manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose \texttt{ReactVLA}, a lightweight and low-latency VLA framework for real-time robotic manipulation. \texttt{ReactVLA} combines two complementary designs: (1) an improved Mean Flow (iMF) action generator that reduces expensive multi-step diffusion sampling to one-to-few-step action generation, and (2) Attention Residuals (AttnRes), a dynamic depth-wise feature routing mechanism that replaces uniform residual accumulation to better preserve task-relevant multimodal representations. We evaluate \texttt{ReactVLA} on large-scale simulation benchmarks, including LIBERO and RoboIMI, as well as real-world robotic manipulation tasks. Experimental results show that \texttt{ReactVLA} consistently outperforms similarly sized VLA baselines, including SmolVLA and $π_0$. On challenging precision manipulation tasks, \texttt{ReactVLA} achieves up to a 1.65$\times$ improvement in task performance while providing more than a 4$\times$ increase in inference speed compared with leading VLA models. Finally, it reduces real-world policy latency to below 38.6 ms, enabling fast reactive control on physical robot platforms. Please check out our project website at: https://game-loader.github.io/ReactVLA/.

AI.tldr: ReactVLA is a lightweight, low-latency VLA framework for real-time robotic manipulation that combines an improved Mean Flow (iMF) action generator (reducing diffusion sampling to 1-few steps) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes) for dynamic feature routing. It achieves up to 1.65× task improvement and 4× inference speedup over baselines like SmolVLA and π₀, with real-world latency below 38.6 ms.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based VLA policies suffer from high inference latency due to iterative sampling, limiting their use in reactive closed-loop robot manipulation. The goal is to reduce latency while retaining multimodal action expressiveness.
AI.method: ReactVLA introduces (1) iMF (improved Mean Flow) action generator for one-to-few-step action generation, and (2) AttnRes (Attention Residuals), a dynamic depth-wise feature routing mechanism that replaces uniform residual accumulation to preserve task-relevant multimodal representations.
AI.result: Outperforms SmolVLA and π₀ on LIBERO and RoboIMI benchmarks and real-world tasks; up to 1.65× task performance improvement and over 4× inference speed increase; real-world policy latency below 38.6 ms.
AI.conclusion: ReactVLA enables fast reactive control on physical robots by drastically reducing diffusion sampling steps and improving feature routing, making it suitable for real-time closed-loop manipulation.

title: Dense Coordinate-List Fine-Tuning Induces a Controllable Interference Surface in Vision-Language Models
summary: Fine-tuning vision-language models to emit dense coordinate lists improves visual grounding but also changes how models serialize, repeat, and terminate structured outputs. We study this behavior as a generation and control surface. In Gemma 4 12B, high-capacity q/k/v/o LoRA raises class-aware F1@0.3 from 0.007 to 0.448 while inducing repeated-tail pressure (duplicate rate 0.080, max repeat 23). A q/v rank sweep keeps max repeat at 21-22 across ranks 4-64, showing capacity persistence. The target signal is separable: object-level repeat-stop removes exact repeated records (duplicate rate 0.000, max repeat 1) while preserving F1 (0.494 to 0.490) and stricter F1@0.5 (0.381 to 0.385). Structure-axis probes localize the effect to bbox-coordinate object lists; dense non-bbox and spatial/count JSON remain repeat-clean, including under high-capacity adapters. Qwen3-VL-8B reproduces a clean controlled endpoint (F1@0.3 0.318, duplicate rate 0.000), and COCO 2017 reproduces acquisition plus duplicate pressure. Dense coordinate-list adaptation therefore creates a structure-bound, cross-family interference surface that can be measured and controlled.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning VLMs to emit dense coordinate lists improves visual grounding (F1@0.3 0.007→0.448) but introduces structure-bound repetitive-tail pressure; this effect is separable via object-level repeat-stop and localizes specifically to bbox-coordinate lists, not other output structures.
AI.motivation: To study how fine-tuning vision-language models for dense coordinate-list generation changes their serialization, repetition, and termination behavior, treating this as a generation and control surface rather than just a performance metric.
AI.method: Applied high-capacity q/k/v/o LoRA to Gemma 4 12B for dense coordinate prediction; conducted q/v rank sweeps; decomposed the target signal with object-level repeat-stop; used structure-axis probes on bbox vs. non-bbox and spatial/count JSON; validated on Qwen3-VL-8B and COCO 2017.
AI.result: High-capacity LoRA raised F1@0.3 to 0.448 but induced repeated-tail pressure (duplicate rate 0.080, max repeat 23). Rank sweep showed capacity persistence (max repeat 21-22). Repeat-stop preserved F1 (0.490) while eliminating duplicates (0.000). Effect localized to bbox-coordinate lists only. Cross-family reproduction in Qwen3-VL-8B and COCO 2017.
AI.conclusion: Dense coordinate-list adaptation creates a structure-bound, cross-family interference surface that can be measured and controlled through targeted interventions like object-level repeat-stop.

title: FloVerse: Floor Plan-Guided Multi-Modal Navigation
summary: Floor plans encapsulate compact spatial priors, enabling agents to navigate unseen scenes more efficiently. While prior work has explored floor plan-guided navigation, it has focused mainly on PointNav and a limited set of environments. To bridge this gap, we introduce FloVerse, a new task for floor plan-guided embodied navigation that unifies PointNav, ObjectNav, and ImageNav. To support FloVerse, we assemble FloVerse-1.6K, a large-scale dataset of 1.6K scenes from HM3D and Gibson 4+, paired with corresponding floor plans, comprising 240K expert trajectories and 12M RGBD frames. We further propose ThreeDiff, a two-stage imitation learning policy comprising a planner, a diffusion-based multimodal goal-reasoning module trained via masked-modality modeling, and a refiner, a depth-based trajectory-refinement module for safe execution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that (1) floor-plan priors improve navigation performance across all goal modalities, and (2) ThreeDiff implicitly captures spatial information from floor plans. These results underscore the effectiveness of spatial priors and validate our proposed unified approach for floor plan-guided embodied navigation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FloVerse, a unified task for floor plan-guided embodied navigation covering PointNav, ObjectNav, and ImageNav, along with a large-scale dataset (FloVerse-1.6K) and a two-stage imitation learning policy (ThreeDiff) that leverages diffusion-based multimodal goal reasoning and depth-based trajectory refinement, demonstrating that floor plan priors improve navigation across all goal modalities.
AI.motivation: Prior work on floor plan-guided navigation has been limited to PointNav and a narrow set of environments. The authors aim to bridge this gap by unifying multiple navigation tasks (PointNav, ObjectNav, ImageNav) under a single floor plan-guided framework.
AI.method: ThreeDiff is a two-stage imitation learning policy: (1) a planner with a diffusion-based multimodal goal-reasoning module trained via masked-modality modeling, and (2) a refiner, a depth-based trajectory-refinement module for safe execution. The FloVerse-1.6K dataset contains 1.6K scenes with floor plans, 240K expert trajectories, and 12M RGBD frames.
AI.result: Floor plan priors improve navigation performance across all goal modalities (PointNav, ObjectNav, ImageNav). ThreeDiff implicitly captures spatial information from floor plans, validating the effectiveness of spatial priors in embodied navigation.
AI.conclusion: Floor plan-guided navigation can be effectively unified across multiple goal modalities, and the proposed ThreeDiff policy successfully leverages floor plan spatial priors to enhance navigation performance, demonstrating the value of structured spatial information in embodied agents.

title: Every Eval Ever: A Unifying Schema and Community Repository for AI Evaluation Results
summary: AI evaluations are widely used for testing and understanding progress. However, the diverse evaluators bring with them inconsistencies that challenge analysis and comparison. First, results are saved in incompatible formats, scattered across leaderboards, papers, blog posts, evaluation harness logs, and custom repositories. Second, results are created by different evaluation frameworks, which produce divergent scores for nominally identical evaluations and record metadata inconsistently, hindering comparison, cross-community evaluation science, cost reduction, and reuse. We introduce Every Eval Ever, the first shared schema and community-crowdsourced repository for AI evaluation results. The schema standardizes how evaluations are represented in a unified, single JSON document. It is source-agnostic by design, ingesting results from evaluation harnesses and papers alike, and optionally stores per-instance outputs for fine-grained analysis. We contribute: (i) a community-governed metadata schema with a companion instance-level schema, the first standardization effort of its kind; (ii) automatic converters from popular formats, evaluation harnesses, and leaderboards to the unified schema; and (iii) a crowdsourced community database hosted on Hugging Face, currently spanning to date 22,235 models, 2,273 unique benchmarks, and 31 evaluation formats.

AI.tldr: Every Eval Ever is the first shared schema and community-crowdsourced repository for AI evaluation results, providing a unified JSON format, automatic converters from popular evaluation frameworks, and a Hugging Face-hosted database with 22,235 models, 2,273 benchmarks, and 31 evaluation formats.
AI.motivation: Current AI evaluation results are scattered across incompatible formats, leaderboards, papers, and repositories, with inconsistent frameworks producing divergent scores for identical evaluations and hindering comparison, cross-community analysis, cost reduction, and reuse.
AI.method: The authors introduce a community-governed metadata schema with a companion instance-level schema that standardizes evaluation representations into a unified JSON document, along with automatic converters from popular evaluation harnesses and leaderboards, and a crowdsourced community database hosted on Hugging Face.
AI.result: The repository currently spans 22,235 models, 2,273 unique benchmarks, and 31 evaluation formats.
AI.conclusion: Every Eval Ever addresses fragmentation in AI evaluation by providing a source-agnostic, standardized schema and a community-crowdsourced repository that enables consistent comparison and fine-grained analysis across diverse evaluation sources.

title: Robust Fall Recovery for Armless Bipedal-Wheeled Robots Via Force-Guided Learning
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, accepted by IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Fall recovery is critical for autonomous legged locomotion. Existing methods have demonstrated that some legged robots, such as humanoids and quadrupeds, are capable of fall recovery from diverse postures by utilizing arms or coordinating multi-legs to generate support forces. Without arms or other legs to provide supportive assistance, a bipedal-wheeled robot must rely solely on the actuation of its legs, making recovery particularly difficult. To address this, we introduce FTSR (Force-guided Teacher-student framework with Stage-wise Rewards). The force-guided method constructs an external auxiliary force during simulation training that correlates directly with the robot's real-time height, explicitly formulating this force as an optimizable constraint. Through constrained reinforcement learning, the policy is guided toward reducing force dependency gradually and increasing the body height, developing internal recovery strategies despite having no arms for support. Height-progressive stage-Wise rewards progressively structure posture stabilization during recovery and transition to sustained locomotion, integrated with teacher-student architecture distilling privileged knowledge of force effects and recovery dynamics. After simulation training, the policy is deployed on a physical armless bipedal-wheeled robot and extensively evaluated. Experiments confirm robust and reliable fall recovery under diverse challenging conditions, demonstrating strong environmental adaptability and motion robustness, while maintaining full post-recovery motion capability. The framework also generalizes effectively to a high-DOF humanoid, confirming its practical generalizability. The project page is available at https://2350575870.github.io/force-guided.github.io/

AI.tldr: FTSR is a force-guided teacher-student reinforcement learning framework with stage-wise rewards enabling armless bipedal-wheeled robots to recover from falls and transition to locomotion, validated on physical robots and generalized to humanoids.
AI.motivation: Fall recovery for armless bipedal-wheeled robots is particularly difficult because they lack arms or extra legs for support, relying solely on leg actuation. Existing methods for humanoids and quadrupeds leverage arms or multi-leg coordination, which does not apply to this robot morphology.
AI.method: FTSR introduces an external auxiliary force correlated with robot height during simulation training, formulated as an optimizable constraint. Constrained RL guides the policy to reduce force dependency while increasing body height. Height-progressive stage-wise rewards structure posture stabilization and transition to locomotion. Teacher-student architecture distills privileged knowledge of force effects and recovery dynamics.
AI.result: Experiments on a physical armless bipedal-wheeled robot demonstrate robust fall recovery under diverse challenging conditions, with strong environmental adaptability and motion robustness. The method also generalizes effectively to a high-DOF humanoid robot.
AI.conclusion: The force-guided teacher-student framework with stage-wise rewards enables reliable fall recovery for armless bipedal-wheeled robots without requiring supplementary support structures, and shows practical generalizability to other legged robot morphologies.

title: StreamMemBench: Streaming Evaluation of Agent Memory for Future-Oriented Assistance
summary: A central role of personal-agent memory is to turn stored information and prior interactions into future-oriented assistance. In daily use, useful cues come from what the agent observes and how the user interacts with the agent, and the agent must carry them forward from the current request to similar future tasks. Existing memory benchmarks usually test dialogue recall or task improvement in isolation, leaving the trajectory from streaming observations to later assistance largely untested. We introduce StreamMemBench, a streaming benchmark that constructs a two-step task sequence around each evidence anchor from EgoLife egocentric streams. The initial task tests evidence use, while the follow-up task tests whether feedback and interaction experience are reused. Four metrics diagnose evidence recall, initial evidence use, feedback incorporation, and follow-up reuse. Experiments with eight memory systems across two backbones show that current systems often fail to use observed evidence or turn feedback into reliable follow-up behavior, even when evidence is stored or feedback is incorporated locally. StreamMemBench is publicly available at https://github.com/landian60/StreamMemBench.

AI.tldr: StreamMemBench is a streaming benchmark that evaluates personal-agent memory by testing how well agents use evidence from egocentric streams and incorporate user feedback into future tasks, revealing that current memory systems struggle with both evidence recall and feedback-driven follow-up behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks test dialogue recall or task improvement in isolation, failing to evaluate the full trajectory from streaming observations to later assistance in personal-agent contexts.
AI.method: StreamMemBench constructs two-step task sequences around evidence anchors from EgoLife egocentric streams: the initial task tests evidence use, and the follow-up task tests feedback and interaction experience reuse. Four metrics diagnose evidence recall, initial evidence use, feedback incorporation, and follow-up reuse.
AI.result: Experiments across eight memory systems and two backbones show that current systems often fail to use observed evidence or turn feedback into reliable follow-up behavior, even when evidence is stored or feedback is incorporated locally.
AI.conclusion: Current memory systems have significant limitations in streaming memory scenarios, particularly in leveraging observed evidence and translating user feedback into consistent future behavior.

title: Elastic Queries Reinforcement Learning: Self-Aware Policy Execution for VLA Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are powerful action generators for robot manipulation, but they are typically executed with fixed inference and replanning schedules. This rigidity ignores the uneven difficulty of robot control: contact-rich or uncertain states may need more computation and fresher feedback, while easier states can often be handled with fewer inference steps and longer open-loop execution. We propose Elastic Queries Reinforcement Learning (EQRL), a framework that makes each VLA policy query elastic. A lightweight latent-schedule adaptor jointly selects the latent input, denoising budget, and action chunk length, without fine-tuning the underlying VLA model. To make scheduling difficulty-aware, EQRL trains a critic over the joint latent-schedule action and derives a state difficulty signal from critic ensemble disagreement. This signal guides compute toward difficult states, while a learned residual allows task-driven correction. We formulate variable chunk execution as query-level macro-action RL with chunk-dependent discounting and an amortized number-of-function-evaluations (NFE) budget. Across simulation and real-robot manipulation, EQRL reduces amortized inference cost while preserving or improving task success.

AI.tldr: EQRL is a framework that makes VLA policy queries elastic by jointly selecting latent input, denoising budget, and action chunk length based on state difficulty, reducing inference cost while maintaining task success.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models use fixed inference and replanning schedules, ignoring that different robot control states (e.g., contact-rich vs. easy) require varying amounts of computation and feedback frequency.
AI.method: EQRL uses a lightweight latent-schedule adaptor that jointly selects latent input, denoising budget, and action chunk length. A critic trained over joint latent-schedule action derives a state difficulty signal from critic ensemble disagreement, guiding compute allocation. Variable chunk execution is formulated as query-level macro-action RL with chunk-dependent discounting and amortized NFE budget.
AI.result: Across simulation and real-robot manipulation, EQRL reduces amortized inference cost while preserving or improving task success.
AI.conclusion: Making VLA queries elastic via difficulty-aware scheduling can reduce computation without sacrificing performance, offering a practical approach for efficient robot manipulation.

title: VISTA: View-Consistent Self-Verified Training for GUI Grounding
summary: When applying Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for GUI Grounding, rollouts are sampled from a single screenshot view; groups often become either all failures on difficult instances or all successes on easy ones, yielding no useful relative advantage. We propose VISTA (View-Consistent Self-Verified Training), a GRPO-based training framework that constructs each comparison group from multiple target-preserving views of the same GUI instance.Each view is generated by a crop that keeps the target element visible and remaps its box exactly, so model rollouts are compared across semantically equivalent but geometrically different inputs. To stabilize short coordinate generation without turning reinforcement learning into unconditional imitation, VISTA further adds a self-verified cross-view anchor: an oracle answer optimized with an advantage-weighted loss, excluded from the group baseline and activated only when the model has produced a maximum-reward rollout. Across five GUI-grounding benchmarks and multiple Qwen backbones, VISTA consistently improves grounding accuracy.On ScreenSpot-Pro, it raises Qwen3-VL 4B/8B/30B-A3B from 55.5/52.7/53.7 to 63.4/65.8/67.0. Robustness analyses further show higher worst-view accuracy and lower prediction flip rates.

AI.tldr: VISTA improves GUI grounding by constructing GRPO groups from multiple views of the same instance (via target-preserving crops) and adding a self-verified cross-view anchor, achieving consistent gains across benchmarks (e.g., +7.9–13.1% on ScreenSpot-Pro).
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO for GUI grounding samples rollouts from a single screenshot view, causing groups to be uniformly all failures (hard instances) or all successes (easy ones), which yields no useful relative advantage for policy learning.
AI.method: VISTA (1) constructs each comparison group from multiple target-preserving views of the same GUI instance via crops that keep the target visible and remap its box; (2) adds a self-verified cross-view anchor—an oracle answer with advantage-weighted loss, excluded from the group baseline, activated only when the model produces a maximum-reward rollout—to stabilize short coordinate generation without unconditional imitation.
AI.result: Across five GUI-grounding benchmarks and multiple Qwen backbones, VISTA consistently improves accuracy. On ScreenSpot-Pro, Qwen3-VL 4B/8B/30B-A3B rise from 55.5/52.7/53.7 to 63.4/65.8/67.0. Robustness analyses show higher worst-view accuracy and lower prediction flip rates.
AI.conclusion: VISTA effectively addresses the group homogeneity problem in GRPO for GUI grounding by leveraging view diversity and a self-verified anchor, leading to more robust and accurate grounding.

title: Hy-Embodied-0.5-VLA: From Vision-Language-Action Models to a Real-World Robot Learning Stack
summary: In this report, we present Hy-Embodied-0.5-VLA, abbreviated as HyVLA-0.5, an end-to-end system that spans the full robot learning stack: data collection, model design, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning, RL post-training, and real-world deployment. Each component serves a distinct role in this stack.

AI.tldr: HyVLA-0.5 is a full-stack end-to-end robot learning system covering data collection, model design, pre-training, fine-tuning, RL post-training, and real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: To present a complete end-to-end robot learning system that integrates all components from data to deployment.
AI.method: The system comprises six stages: data collection, model design, continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, RL post-training, and real-world deployment.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract; focuses on system architecture rather than empirical results.
AI.conclusion: Each component in the proposed stack plays a distinct role in enabling the full robot learning pipeline.

title: A Temporal Planning Framework for Disruption Aware Dynamic Route Optimization in Heterogeneous Railway Systems
summary: Efficient route optimization play a vital role in ensuring both safety and punctuality in railway operations. It is very crucial particularly in heterogeneous multi-gauge railway networks with varying train speed, stopping pattern, infrastructure compatibility constraints increase coordination complexity. In single-track systems these challenges are further intensify due to all trains to share the same track and requires frequent track switching.Stochastic disruptions events including blocked tracks, blocked trains, engine failure and speed slowdowns introduces additional unpredictability in operations and deviate the timetable. However, existing studies predominantly focuses on high-level timetabling, omitting operational details such as track switching coordination. As a result leaving decision to human operators, increasing safety risks into railway operations. This study proposes a framework based on temporal planning for dynamic route optimization and disruption management in heterogeneous railway systems. The framework formulates railway operations as a temporal planning problem using PDDL 2.1 with explicitly modeling gauge compatibility constraints and diverse disruption scenarios. It generates conflict-free timestamped operational plans specifying both optimized schedules and executable action sequences. To evaluate the proposed framework, we developed a benchmark problem set with 200 instances using up to 1,000 track points and 120 trains. Two state-of-the-art temporal planners and a plan validator were employed to assessed the framework. The experimental results demonstrate that the framework effectively generates temporal operational plans for heterogeneous railway systems and handles multi-gauge constraints, disruptions, and reduces dependence on manual decision making.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a temporal planning framework (PDDL 2.1) for dynamic route optimization and disruption management in heterogeneous multi-gauge railway networks, explicitly modeling gauge compatibility, track switching, and stochastic disruptions. Evaluated on 200 benchmark instances (up to 1,000 track points, 120 trains) using two planners and a validator, it generates conflict-free timestamped operational plans and reduces reliance on manual decision-making.
AI.motivation: Existing studies focus on high-level timetabling but omit operational details like track switching coordination, leaving decisions to human operators and increasing safety risks. Stochastic disruptions (blocked tracks, engine failure, speed slowdowns) further complicate operations in heterogeneous multi-gauge, single-track systems.
AI.method: Formulates railway operations as a temporal planning problem using PDDL 2.1, explicitly modeling gauge compatibility constraints and diverse disruption scenarios. Generates conflict-free timestamped operational plans with optimized schedules and executable action sequences.
AI.result: Tested on 200 benchmark instances (up to 1,000 track points, 120 trains) using two state-of-the-art temporal planners and a plan validator. The framework effectively generates temporal operational plans, handles multi-gauge constraints and disruptions, and reduces dependence on manual decision-making.
AI.conclusion: The proposed temporal planning framework successfully addresses dynamic route optimization and disruption management in heterogeneous railway systems, improving safety and punctuality by automating coordination tasks previously left to human operators.

title: ForestBack: Breadcrumb-Based Pedestrian Dead Reckoning for Infrastructure-Free Return Navigation
summary: Reliable return navigation remains an important challenge in GPS-denied environments where external positioning infrastructure may be unavailable or unreliable. This paper presents ForestBack, an infrastructure-free pedestrian return navigation framework based on breadcrumb-based pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR). The system records a user's walking route as a sequence of reversible breadcrumb nodes and generates reverse-path guidance without requiring GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth beacons, or pre-installed infrastructure. ForestBack integrates acceleration-based step detection, adaptive step-length estimation, magnetometer-assisted heading estimation, barometric-altitude correction, and bidirectional breadcrumb path reconstruction. The system was evaluated using an indoor obstacle-avoidance route with five checkpoints, where the user navigated around a central obstacle. A dataset of 36 walking trials and 42,474 time-series samples was used for evaluation, including IMU signals, magnetometer readings, barometric variables, turn-event labels, ground-truth trajectories, baseline PDR outputs, proposed ForestBack outputs, and power-related measurements. Experimental results show that ForestBack reduced the mean RMSE from 1.129 m to 0.965 m compared with traditional PDR, corresponding to a 15.76% improvement. The mean final-position error was reduced from 1.781 m to 1.388 m, while turn-event detection consistency reached approximately 99.90%. These results indicate that ForestBack improves trajectory reconstruction and route-preserving return guidance in obstacle-avoidance scenarios. The released dataset and analysis notebook support reproducibility and future benchmarking of infrastructure-free PDR-based return navigation systems.

AI.tldr: ForestBack is an infrastructure-free pedestrian return navigation framework using breadcrumb-based PDR that reduces mean RMSE from 1.129m to 0.965m (15.76% improvement) and achieves 99.90% turn-event detection consistency for reliable return guidance in GPS-denied environments.
AI.motivation: Reliable return navigation in GPS-denied environments is challenging due to the lack of external positioning infrastructure (GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth beacons). The paper aims to develop an infrastructure-free solution that enables pedestrians to navigate back along their original route without requiring pre-installed infrastructure.
AI.method: ForestBack employs a breadcrumb-based PDR framework that records walking routes as reversible breadcrumb nodes. It integrates acceleration-based step detection, adaptive step-length estimation, magnetometer-assisted heading estimation, barometric-altitude correction, and bidirectional breadcrumb path reconstruction. Evaluation used 36 walking trials (42,474 samples) on an indoor obstacle-avoidance route with five checkpoints.
AI.result: ForestBack reduced mean RMSE from 1.129m to 0.965m (15.76% improvement), reduced mean final-position error from 1.781m to 1.388m, and achieved ~99.90% turn-event detection consistency compared to traditional PDR.
AI.conclusion: ForestBack improves trajectory reconstruction and route-preserving return guidance in obstacle-avoidance scenarios. The released dataset and analysis notebook support reproducibility and future benchmarking of infrastructure-free PDR-based return navigation systems.

title: Abstracting Cross-Domain Action Sequences into Interpretable Workflows
summary: Sequential or time-stamped interaction logs provide objective records of digital application usage, yet their granularity and noise often obscure meaningful insights into people's work. Such insights are essential for improving digital products in ways grounded in real-world user interactions. Prior research has applied deep learning models to cluster user actions into high-level activities, but these approaches are highly sensitive to noise and struggle to generalize across applications. To address this limitation, we introduce WorkflowView, a framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to abstract low-level action sequences into high-level activities. We establish the effectiveness and generality of our approach across three distinct, challenging sequential tasks and diverse domains: (a) zero-shot task description reconstruction from browser logs (achieving high semantic similarity, $μ_{sim} = 0.91$), (b) few-shot student dropout prediction using MOOC interaction logs (reaching weighted $F_1 = 0.90$ with only five few-shot examples), and (c) anonymized, privacy-preserving analysis of AI tool integration within document workflows in Microsoft Word. Our work demonstrates that LLM-based abstraction is a robust and efficient path forward for transforming low-level behavioral data into high-level, interpretable, and actionable insights. We also discuss practical considerations for deploying LLM-based inferences within logging infrastructures, including computational efficiency and user privacy.

AI.tldr: WorkflowView leverages LLMs to transform noisy, low-level user interaction logs into high-level, interpretable activities, demonstrating effectiveness across browser logs, MOOC dropout prediction, and privacy-preserving AI tool analysis in Microsoft Word.
AI.motivation: Time-stamped interaction logs provide objective records but their granularity and noise obscure meaningful insights into people's work, which are needed for improving digital products. Prior deep learning approaches are sensitive to noise and struggle to generalize across applications.
AI.method: A framework (WorkflowView) that uses large language models (LLMs) to abstract low-level action sequences into high-level activities.
AI.result: Zero-shot task description reconstruction from browser logs (μ_sim=0.91), few-shot student dropout prediction from MOOC logs (F1=0.90 with five examples), and anonymized privacy-preserving analysis of AI tool integration in Microsoft Word workflows.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based abstraction is a robust and efficient path forward for transforming low-level behavioral data into high-level, interpretable, and actionable insights. Practical considerations for deployment (computational efficiency, user privacy) are also discussed.

title: Kine2Go: Kinematic dataset for the Unitree Go2 robot with diverse gaits and motions
summary: The recent popularity of robotics, combined with the steadily decreasing cost of robotic hardware, has lowered the entry barrier to robotics research and enabled rapid advancements in the field. One of the primary examples is the Unitree Go2 quadruped robot, which is often used by researchers in the areas of locomotion, navigation, control, and others. Many researchers use the Go2 robot in combination with techniques like imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and behavioral cloning to allow machine learning systems to take full control of the robot. At the same time, many of those techniques require demonstration data consisting of the robot's kinematics information and actions applied to the motors. Obtaining such data is difficult, requires building complex pipelines, and can take significant time. To aid in those kinds of efforts, we present Kine2Go - a dataset with 800 diverse gait kinematics trajectory motion data for the Unitree Go2 robot, derived from 40 distinct policies. Our pipeline accepts data from various quadruped morphologies and translates them to a Go2-compatible format. Then we use Reinforcement Learning to train policies following a given motion, and finally we gather data from those policies, which grants robust, perturbed kinematic data with corresponding motor-level actions.

AI.tldr: Kine2Go is a dataset of 800 diverse gait kinematics trajectories for the Unitree Go2 quadruped robot, derived from 40 policies via Reinforcement Learning, designed to provide robust kinematic data with motor-level actions for imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and behavioral cloning research.
AI.motivation: Obtaining demonstration data (kinematics + motor actions) for the Unitree Go2 robot is difficult, requires complex pipelines, and is time-consuming, hindering research in imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and behavioral cloning.
AI.method: The pipeline accepts gait data from various quadruped morphologies, translates them to Go2-compatible format, uses Reinforcement Learning to train policies that follow given motions, and then gathers robust perturbed kinematic data with corresponding motor-level actions from those policies.
AI.result: A dataset containing 800 diverse gait kinematics trajectory motion data for the Unitree Go2 robot, derived from 40 distinct policies.
AI.conclusion: Kine2Go lowers the barrier for robotics researchers by providing accessible demonstration data for the Go2 quadruped, enabling easier application of machine learning techniques requiring kinematics and motor action data.

title: Towards Direct Latent-Space Synthesis for Parallel Branches in LLM-Agent Workflows
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as execution engines for agentic systems, yet they still consume context through a sequential text interface. This creates a mismatch with modern structured agent workflows, in which independent branches explore subtasks, retrieve evidence, or generate candidate solutions before a final synthesis step. Existing systems typically merge these branches by concatenating their textual outputs, which discards the parallel structure and incurs redundant prefill computation. In this work, we introduce Parallel-Synthesis, a plug-and-play framework that enables a synthesizer to directly consume the KV caches produced by parallel worker agents. Parallel-Synthesis combines a cache mapper that calibrates independently generated branch caches with a fine-tuned synthesizer adapter that enables generation from this non-sequential cache interface. We train Parallel-Synthesis using data that exposes the synthesizer to parallel cache contexts, teaches aggregation across cached branches, and distills reasoning behavior from standard text-concatenation-based synthesis. Across nine downstream datasets spanning math, science QA, code generation, GAIA, and multi-agent database diagnosis, Parallel-Synthesis matches or outperforms text-based synthesis on seven datasets and remains close on the other two. It also reduces time-to-first-token by 2.5x-11x, suggesting that direct cache-based synthesis is a promising interface for more native and efficient synthesis over parallel agent branches.

AI.tldr: Parallel-Synthesis is a plug-and-play framework that enables language model synthesizers to directly consume KV caches from parallel worker agents, bypassing sequential text concatenation. It matches or outperforms text-based synthesis on 7/9 datasets while reducing time-to-first-token by 2.5x–11x.
AI.motivation: There is a mismatch between sequential text interfaces of LLMs and modern structured agent workflows where parallel branches explore subtasks, retrieve evidence, or generate candidates. Existing concatenation-based merging discards parallel structure and incurs redundant prefill computation.
AI.method: Parallel-Synthesis combines a cache mapper that calibrates independently generated branch caches with a fine-tuned synthesizer adapter that enables generation from non-sequential cache interfaces. Training data exposes the synthesizer to parallel cache contexts, teaches aggregation across cached branches, and distills reasoning from text-concatenation-based synthesis.
AI.result: Across math, science QA, code generation, GAIA, and multi-agent database diagnosis (9 datasets), Parallel-Synthesis matches or outperforms text-based synthesis on 7 datasets and remains close on the other two, while reducing time-to-first-token by 2.5x–11x.
AI.conclusion: Direct cache-based synthesis is a promising interface for more native and efficient synthesis over parallel agent branches.

title: CADET: Physics-Grounded Causal Auditing and Training-Free Deconfounding of End-to-End Driving Planners
summary: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous-driving planners trained by imitation are prone to statistical shortcuts: they associate scene elements that merely co-occur with expert actions (a roadside object, a building facade) with driving decisions, rather than the variables that causally determine them. Such causal confusion silently compromises reliability in long-tail scenarios, and it is difficult to detect, because prevailing open-loop metrics (L2 displacement and collision rate) are dominated by ego status and do not indicate whether a planner depends on spurious cues. Existing remedies based on causal-intervention training require retraining large models and cannot audit a planner that is already deployed. We present CADET, a training-free framework that audits, benchmarks, and repairs spurious reliance in pretrained E2E planners without any parameter update.

AI.tldr: CADET is a training-free framework that audits, benchmarks, and repairs spurious causal confusion in pretrained end-to-end autonomous driving planners without parameter updates.
AI.motivation: E2E autonomous-driving planners trained by imitation suffer from statistical shortcuts (causal confusion), associating co-occurring but non-causal scene elements with driving decisions. This silently compromises reliability in long-tail scenarios, and existing open-loop metrics fail to detect such spurious dependencies. Current remedies require retraining, which is impractical for deployed models.
AI.method: CADET is a training-free framework that audits, benchmarks, and repairs spurious reliance in pretrained E2E planners without any parameter update.
AI.result: CADET can detect causal confusion (spurious correlations) in deployed planners, benchmark them effectively, and repair the spurious reliance without retraining.
AI.conclusion: CADET offers a practical solution for auditing and fixing causal confusion in already-deployed E2E autonomous driving planners, addressing a critical safety issue in long-tail scenarios without requiring costly retraining.

title: AERMANI-PLACE: Language Guided Object Placement with Aerial Manipulators
summary:
Object placement is a fundamental component of aerial manipulation tasks, yet existing systems typically require the desired placement position to be specified explicitly in metric coordinates. Such interfaces are not intuitive and require users to reason about coordinate frames and scene geometry, making them difficult to use in practical deployments. In contrast, humans often communicate spatial goals through a combination of language and pointing gestures. Inspired by this observation, we present AERMANI-PLACE, a framework for language-guided object placement with aerial manipulators. Given a scene image and a natural language instruction, an image editing model generates a modified version of the scene containing a visual marker that indicates where the object should be placed. This marker is then grounded into the physical environment using depth observations to recover a metric place point, after which a placement trajectory is generated and executed by the aerial manipulator. We evaluate the proposed approach on a test set of 100 language-guided placement tasks and demonstrate successful execution on a real aerial manipulation platform. Experimental results show that the proposed method reliably infers placement locations from language instructions with an average success rate of 87\% on the test-set and transfers effectively to real-world aerial manipulation with an average success rate of 72\%.
  Video: https://youtu.be/SgwwgLBsv0g

AI.tldr: AERMANI-PLACE is a framework for language-guided object placement with aerial manipulators that uses an image editing model to generate visual markers from natural language instructions, which are then grounded into physical 3D coordinates via depth observations for execution. It achieves 87% success on test set and 72% on real-world aerial manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing aerial manipulation placement systems require explicit metric coordinate specifications, which are unintuitive and difficult for users. The authors aim to create a more intuitive interface inspired by how humans communicate spatial goals using language and gestures.
AI.method: Given a scene image and natural language instruction, an image editing model generates a modified scene with a visual marker indicating the placement location. The marker is grounded into physical 3D space using depth observations, then a placement trajectory is generated and executed by the aerial manipulator.
AI.result: 87% average success rate on a test set of 100 language-guided placement tasks, and 72% average success rate on a real aerial manipulation platform.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method reliably infers placement locations from language instructions and transfers effectively to real-world aerial manipulation, offering a more intuitive human-robot interaction paradigm for aerial placement tasks.

title: Spatially Conditioned Diffusion Policy: Learning Precise and Robust Manipulation with a Single RGB Camera
summary: Recent visual imitation learning systems have widely adopted multi-camera setups with wrist-mounted cameras as the de facto standard. However, manipulation from a single global view remains challenging, as the policy should capture fine-grained interaction details and identify task-relevant regions without local wrist views. To address this challenge, we present Spatially Conditioned Diffusion Policy (SCDP), a diffusion-based visuomotor policy that achieves precise and robust manipulation in a single-camera setting. Our key idea is that end-effector trajectories can serve as visual attention anchors that reflect task-relevant regions. Building on this idea, SCDP consists of two key components: (i) a visual encoder that produces multi-scale feature maps to capture both broader context and fine-grained visual features, and (ii) a spatial conditioning module that samples point-wise features along intermediate end-effector trajectories in the diffusion loop. Extensive simulation experiments show that SCDP consistently outperforms strong single-view baselines and achieves performance comparable to multi-camera baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate precise manipulation and robustness to visual distractors, highlighting the potential of single-camera imitation learning.

AI.tldr: SCDP is a diffusion-based visuomotor policy that achieves precise single-camera manipulation by using end-effector trajectories as visual attention anchors to sample point-wise features along predicted trajectories during denoising.
AI.motivation: Multi-camera setups (especially wrist-mounted) are standard for visual imitation learning, but single-camera manipulation struggles to capture fine-grained interaction details and identify task-relevant regions without local views. The authors aim to close this gap.
AI.method: SCDP uses (i) a visual encoder producing multi-scale feature maps for broad context and fine details, and (ii) a spatial conditioning module that samples point-wise features along intermediate end-effector trajectories within the diffusion denoising loop, using trajectories as attention anchors.
AI.result: Simulation experiments show SCDP consistently outperforms strong single-view baselines and achieves performance comparable to multi-camera baselines. Real-world experiments demonstrate precise manipulation and robustness to visual distractors.
AI.conclusion: SCDP demonstrates that single-camera imitation learning can be highly effective, leveraging trajectory-conditioned spatial attention to rival multi-camera performance, highlighting potential for simpler setups.

title: TRACE: Trajectory-Routed Causal Memory for Delayed-Evidence Visuomotor Imitation
summary: Robots under autonomous operation may require decisions based on evidence that is no longer visible. We study \emph{delayed-evidence} tasks, where an early cue disappears before a later decision point, so visually similar observations can require different actions. In these settings, the current observation is not a sufficient state for control. We introduce TRAjectory-routed Causal Evidence (TRACE), a memory framework for visuomotor imitation policies. TRACE stores task-relevant visual and robot-state evidence, such as object identity, target choice, or route-dependent state, in a fixed-size latent memory that remains bounded over long episodes. Instead of indexing memory by raw time or manually provided task labels, TRACE uses \emph{path signatures}: compact, order-sensitive features of the executed robot-state trajectory. These signatures do not store the visual cue itself; rather, they provide trajectory-conditioned keys for writing and retrieving the evidence stored when the cue was visible. When the robot later reaches an ambiguous observation, the policy conditions on TRACE memory to recover the missing context and choose the correct branch. TRACE attaches through lightweight adapters to policies, without changing the policy backbone, action head, or imitation objective. Across real-world long-horizon manipulation tasks with visually ambiguous branch points, TRACE improves branch selection and task success over alternative baselines, including short-history and recurrent memory. Project page: https://jeong-zju.github.io/trace

AI.tldr: TRACE is a memory framework for visuomotor imitation policies that uses path signatures of robot trajectories to store and retrieve task-relevant visual evidence from earlier time steps, enabling correct decision-making at later ambiguous branch points where the original visual cue is no longer visible.
AI.motivation: Robots operating autonomously often face delayed-evidence tasks where an early visual cue disappears before a later decision point, making the current observation insufficient for control. Standard policies lack memory mechanisms to retain this critical information across time.
AI.method: TRACE stores visual and state evidence in fixed-size latent memory indexed by path signatures (compact, order-sensitive trajectory features) rather than raw time or labels. These signatures serve as write/retrieve keys for evidence stored when the cue was visible, allowing the policy to condition on missing context at ambiguous observations.
AI.result: On real-world long-horizon manipulation tasks with visually ambiguous branch points, TRACE improves branch selection and task success over baselines including short-history and recurrent memory approaches.
AI.conclusion: TRACE provides an effective, lightweight memory solution for delayed-evidence tasks by using trajectory-conditioned signatures to store and retrieve relevant visual cues, without modifying the policy backbone or training objective.

title: ORCA: A Platform for Open-Source Dexterity Research
summary: Robotics manipulation research increasingly focuses on two-finger parallel grippers for their effectiveness, affordability, and ease of teleoperation. Grippers are nonetheless limited by their form factor, often requiring bimanual setups even for simple reorientation tasks.
