Anthropomorphic hands are a more natural platform for dexterous robot learning -- closer to the human hand, and capable of learning from human video -- yet they remain hard to use in learning research: even where open and accessible hand hardware exists, the software for control, simulation, teleoperation, and retargeting is scattered in one-off code bases, and largely disconnected from the robot-learning ecosystem. In this work, we introduce the \orca~learning stack, an open-source research stack for dexterity as a first-class robot learning domain. Our \orca~stack unifies low-level control, simulation, teleoperation from a range of consumer platforms, and hand retargeting, behind a single interface, and integrates natively with popular robot-learning frameworks such as \lerobot, so dexterous hand researchers can leverage the same data, training, and evaluation pipelines used for non-dexterous robot learning. We demonstrate a complete end-to-end workflow, collecting expert demonstrations of an in-hand reorientation task by teleoperation with a consumer-grade VR headset, training an autonomous policy with \lerobot, and evaluating the learned policy in a fully reproducible and observable setup. We open-source the entire stack as a shared, reproducible foundation for dexterous-manipulation research.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ORCA, an open-source research stack that unifies control, simulation, teleoperation, and retargeting for dexterous robotic manipulation with anthropomorphic hands, integrating with existing robot learning frameworks to enable reproducible dexterity research.
AI.motivation: Two-finger parallel grippers dominate robotics manipulation research but are limited in dexterity, often requiring bimanual setups even for simple reorientation. Anthropomorphic hands offer a more natural platform for dexterous learning and can leverage human video data, but the software ecosystem for control, simulation, teleoperation, and retargeting is fragmented, disconnected from mainstream robot-learning frameworks, hindering progress in dexterity research.
AI.method: The authors build the ORCA learning stack, an open-source system that unifies low-level control, simulation, teleoperation from consumer platforms (e.g., VR headsets), and hand retargeting behind a single interface. It integrates natively with popular robot-learning frameworks like LeRobot, allowing dexterous hand researchers to reuse existing data, training, and evaluation pipelines. They demonstrate an end-to-end workflow: collecting expert demonstrations of in-hand reorientation via VR teleoperation, training a policy with LeRobot, and evaluating it in a reproducible setup.
AI.result: A complete end-to-end workflow is demonstrated: expert demonstrations of in-hand reorientation collected via consumer VR teleoperation, an autonomous policy trained using LeRobot, and evaluated in a fully reproducible and observable setup. The entire stack is open-sourced as a shared foundation for the research community.
AI.conclusion: ORCA provides a unified, open-source software stack that makes dexterous manipulation with anthropomorphic hands a first-class domain in robot learning, enabling researchers to leverage existing robot-learning pipelines and reproducible experimental setups.

title: Sensitivity Shaping for Latent Modeling
summary: Generative dynamics models enable planning in challenging robotic systems, but safe deployment requires reliably detecting policy-induced out-of-distribution (OOD) transitions. Existing methods typically treat the learned dynamics as fixed and attach post hoc support surrogates. We show that these surrogates can fail when the dynamics are locally insensitive to critical action choices: unsupported control actions may produce latent predictions that resemble demonstrated transitions, suppressing OOD signals despite large true predictive errors. To address this, we introduce support-conditioned control-sensitivity regularization, which promotes sensitive local response to control input changes in learned dynamics in high-support training regions. This preserves control-induced variation while limiting unstable extrapolation due to weak empirical support. Experiments in vision-based obstacle avoidance, manipulation, and real-robot navigation show improved OOD detection and safer closed-loop planning.

AI.tldr: Existing OOD detection methods fail when learned dynamics are locally insensitive to critical control actions; the paper proposes support-conditioned control-sensitivity regularization to improve OOD detection and safer planning in robotic systems.
AI.motivation: Post hoc OOD detection surrogates attached to learned dynamics models can fail when the dynamics are locally insensitive to critical action choices—unsupported control actions may produce latent predictions resembling demonstrated transitions, suppressing OOD signals despite large true predictive errors.
AI.method: Support-conditioned control-sensitivity regularization that promotes sensitive local response to control input changes in high-support training regions, preserving control-induced variation while limiting unstable extrapolation due to weak empirical support.
AI.result: Experiments in vision-based obstacle avoidance, manipulation, and real-robot navigation show improved OOD detection and safer closed-loop planning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed regularization improves OOD detection reliability in learned generative dynamics models, enabling safer deployment in robotic planning tasks.

title: What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI
comment: Accepted in the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026), Kitakyushu, Fukuoka, Japan
summary: Socially assistive robots (SARs) are increasingly deployed in educational and information-sharing contexts, supported by advances in large language models that enable fluent real-time interaction. Despite the growing diversity of robot embodiments, it remains unclear whether a single robot appearance is appropriate across different interaction tasks or whether trust depends primarily on contextual factors. In this study, we examine how robot appearance and task type jointly influence trust in robots. Using a within-subjects video-based experiment (N = 81), participants evaluated three robots with distinct appearances while performing three educationally relevant tasks: teaching, procedural instruction, and personal-information discussion. Results from repeated-measures analyses show a strong main effect of task on trust, with participants reporting the highest trust during instructional guidance, moderate trust during teaching activities, and significantly lower trust when robots requested personal information. In contrast, robot appearance showed no significant main effect, and the interaction between appearance and task was marginal. These findings suggest that trust in human-robot interaction is shaped more strongly by task context than by physical embodiment alone. By focusing on future educators as end users, this work contributes empirical evidence toward task-aware robot deployment in educational environments and highlights the importance of aligning robot roles and behaviors with interaction goals rather than relying solely on anthropomorphic design.

AI.tldr: Trust in social robots is more strongly influenced by task context than robot appearance; participants trusted robots most during instructional tasks and least when asked for personal information, with no significant effect of robot embodiment.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing diversity of robot embodiments, it remains unclear whether a single robot appearance is appropriate across different interaction tasks or whether trust depends primarily on contextual factors.
AI.method: Within-subjects video-based experiment (N=81) where participants evaluated three robots with distinct appearances across three tasks (teaching, procedural instruction, personal-information discussion), analyzed using repeated-measures analyses.
AI.result: Strong main effect of task on trust (highest for instructional guidance, moderate for teaching, lowest for personal-information requests); no significant main effect of robot appearance; marginal interaction between appearance and task.
AI.conclusion: Trust in human-robot interaction is shaped more strongly by task context than physical embodiment alone; task-aware robot deployment should be prioritized over relying solely on anthropomorphic design.

title: Impedance MPC with Disturbance Estimation for Dexterous Hand Control
summary: Dexterous hands must simultaneously track precise finger trajectories and maintain safe, compliant contact -- objectives in tension for any fixed-gain controller. We present an actuator-agnostic Impedance Model Predictive Control (Impedance MPC) framework for dexterous fingers, instantiating the constant-$A_d$ offset-free architecture established for physical human-robot interaction (pHRI); its stability, recursive-feasibility, and input-to-state-stability guarantees are inherited by preserving the architectural assumptions. An algebraic feedforward reduces the tendon transmission -- hydraulic, cable, pneumatic, twisted-string, or series-elastic -- to a constant-coefficient double integrator, so the QP cost inverse is precomputed offline and a 10-step receding-horizon quadratic program runs at 500\,Hz while enforcing hard constraints on contact force (ISO/TS 15066), actuation limits, and jerk. An encoder-only augmented-Kalman disturbance state drives steady-state error to zero under any constant contact load. On a hydraulically actuated finger -- the worked example platform, adding pressure and cavitation constraints -- the 500\,Hz Kalman MPC attains 0.5\,mrad RMS, 0.1\,mrad steady-state, and 6.6\,mrad peak deflection under 1.5\,Nm contact: 183$\times$, 1500$\times$, and 23$\times$ better than classical impedance. The realized first-move stiffness (18$\to$323\,Nm/rad with update rate) is independently verified. The architecture scales to a 16-DOF LEAP Hand MuJoCo simulation, recovering from 2.5\,N grasp-load disturbances within 0.7\,s.

AI.tldr: Impedance MPC framework for dexterous fingers achieves high-precision trajectory tracking (0.5 mrad RMS) and compliant contact simultaneously, outperforming classical impedance by up to 1500× in steady-state error, with stability guarantees inherited from pHRI literature, running at 500 Hz on a hydraulically actuated finger.
AI.motivation: Dexterous hands need to balance precise trajectory tracking with safe, compliant contact, but fixed-gain controllers cannot resolve this tension. Existing methods lack a unified framework that provides both high-fidelity tracking and guaranteed stability under physical contact constraints.
AI.method: Impedance MPC built on the constant-Ad offset-free pHRI architecture, with algebraic feedforward that reduces any tendon transmission to a constant-coefficient double integrator. The QP cost inverse is precomputed offline, enabling a 10-step receding-horizon QP at 500 Hz with hard constraints on contact force (ISO/TS 15066), actuation limits, and jerk. An encoder-only augmented-Kalman disturbance state eliminates steady-state error under constant contact loads.
AI.result: On a hydraulically actuated finger: 0.5 mrad RMS, 0.1 mrad steady-state, 6.6 mrad peak deflection under 1.5 Nm contact—183×, 1500×, and 23× better than classical impedance. Stiffness tunable from 18 to 323 Nm/rad with update rate. In MuJoCo simulation of a 16-DOF LEAP Hand, recovers from 2.5 N grasp-load disturbances within 0.7 s.
AI.conclusion: The Impedance MPC framework provides an actuator-agnostic, stable, and high-performance solution for dexterous manipulation, unifying precise tracking and compliant safety with demonstrated superiority over classical impedance control.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning of Autonomous Highway Driving: A Unified Framework for Safety and Efficiency
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) offers a compelling route to decision-making for advanced autonomous vehicles (AVs), yet its trial-and-error nature makes it difficult to guarantee safety during training and to achieve both safety and efficiency at deployment. We propose a unified safe reinforcement learning (SRL) framework that integrates safe distance (SD), reward machines (RM), and mixture-of-experts (MoE), termed MoE-RM-SRL. For deployment, SD and RM jointly shape a rule-aware reward that encodes highway traffic regulations and stage-wise objectives, enabling safe and reliable behavior without sacrificing efficiency. For training, we introduce a sparsely gated MoE layer comprising up to 11 deep Q-networks (DQNs); an SD-based gating rule activates a minimal set of experts for lane-keeping and lane-changing, mitigating the instability, discontinuities, and impulsive transients commonly induced by switching between heterogeneous controllers (e.g., MPC/rule-based modules and learned policies). We implement the proposed architecture in CARLA and integrate it with a 6-DoF driver-in-the-loop virtual-reality (DiL-VR) platform. Experiments in stochastic two-lane traffic show that MoE-RM-SRL substantially improves safety and efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines, and the framework naturally extends to multi-lane driving as well as on-ramp merging and exiting scenarios.

AI.tldr: MoE-RM-SRL unifies safe distance, reward machines, and mixture-of-experts (sparsely gated DQNs) to achieve both safety and efficiency in autonomous driving, outperforming baselines in CARLA DiL-VR simulations.
AI.motivation: DRL offers a promising route for AV decision-making, but its trial-and-error nature makes it difficult to guarantee safety during training and to achieve both safety and efficiency at deployment.
AI.method: A unified SRL framework integrating safe distance (SD), reward machines (RM), and a sparsely gated mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer of up to 11 DQNs. SD and RM shape a rule-aware reward for deployment; an SD-based gating rule activates minimal experts for lane-keeping/changing to mitigate instability from heterogeneous controller switching.
AI.result: In stochastic two-lane traffic experiments in CARLA with a 6-DoF DiL-VR platform, MoE-RM-SRL substantially improves safety and efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines, and extends to multi-lane, on-ramp merging, and exiting scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the safety-efficiency trade-off in DRL-based AV decision-making, both during training and deployment, and generalizes across diverse driving scenarios.

title: Whole-Body Impedance Model Predictive Control for Safe Physical Human--Robot Interaction on Floating-Base Platforms
summary: Floating-base robots must balance under rigid contact constraints while interacting safely with humans. Existing whole-body control~(WBC) frameworks allocate the full joint space to locomotion or rely on fixed-gain impedance feedback that accumulates steady-state error under sustained physical human--robot interaction~(pHRI) forces. This paper extends the authors' fixed-base two-layer Impedance MPC to floating-base platforms through a three-level architecture: a centroidal MPC plans contact forces over a 500\,ms horizon; a priority-driven WBC layer resolves balance into joint torques through contact-consistent null-space projection; and the residual null space is governed by a receding-horizon quadratic program~(QP) that predicts and rejects pHRI disturbances using a Kalman-augmented state. A contact-consistent feedback linearization reduces the arm end-effector plant to a double integrator with a \emph{constant} state matrix within each contact mode, enabling offline precomputation of the QP cost and ${\geq}1$\,kHz operation. A covariance-inflation protocol preserves the disturbance estimate across contact-mode switches, guaranteeing zero steady-state error under bounded constant pHRI loads, and an Impedance Equivalence Theorem shows the infinite-horizon limit recovers a classical task-space impedance law whose effective mass, damping, and stiffness adapt to posture and contact configuration. Simulations on a 17-DOF biped and the Unitree G1 humanoid validate the design.

AI.tldr: A three-level Impedance MPC framework for floating-base robots that combines centroidal MPC, priority-driven WBC, and receding-horizon QP with Kalman-augmented state estimation to achieve zero steady-state error under sustained human interaction forces while maintaining balance and enabling 1+ kHz real-time operation.
AI.motivation: Existing WBC frameworks either allocate full joint space to locomotion or use fixed-gain impedance feedback that accumulates steady-state error under sustained pHRI forces; this work extends fixed-base Impedance MPC to floating-base platforms to address these limitations.
AI.method: Three-level architecture: (1) centroidal MPC plans contact forces over 500 ms horizon; (2) priority-driven WBC resolves balance into joint torques via contact-consistent null-space projection; (3) residual null space governed by a receding-horizon QP that predicts/rejects pHRI disturbances using Kalman-augmented state. Contact-consistent feedback linearization reduces arm end-effector to a double integrator with constant state matrix per contact mode, enabling offline QP cost precomputation. Covariance-inflation protocol preserves disturbance estimates across contact switches.
AI.result: Validated on a 17-DOF biped and Unitree G1 humanoid via simulation; achieves ≥1 kHz operation through offline precomputation; Impedance Equivalence Theorem proves infinite-horizon limit recovers adaptive task-space impedance law.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework guarantees zero steady-state error under bounded constant pHRI loads while maintaining balance, with the Impedance Equivalence Theorem linking the finite-horizon MPC to classical impedance control with posture/contact-dependent effective mass, damping, and stiffness.

title: EgoGuide: Egocentric Guidance for Efficient Robot-Free Demonstration Collection and Learning
summary: Robot learning from real-world demonstrations is currently constrained by data scaling. Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) provides an efficient robot-free data collection interface, yet current UMI-style pipelines often collect redundant demonstrations and lack global scene context. To improve data efficiency, we present EgoGuide, a collection interface that records synchronized wrist and head/egocentric observations and couples them with online visual-geometric data quality guidance. We also introduce a Gated Egocentric Residual Policy for robust learning from a viewpoint-varying egocentric camera, allowing head/egocentric context to correct ambiguous local observations while preserving stable wrist-view control. Real-world experiments show that EgoGuide reduces the required number of data episodes and improves data efficiency. The residual policy further improves robustness under visual occlusion. Project Page: https://silicx.github.io/EgoGuide

AI.tldr: EgoGuide is a robot-free data collection interface that uses synchronized wrist and egocentric cameras with online data quality guidance, paired with a Gated Egocentric Residual Policy to improve data efficiency and robustness in robot learning from demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Current UMI-style pipelines collect redundant demonstrations and lack global scene context, limiting data efficiency in robot learning from real-world demonstrations.
AI.method: EgoGuide records synchronized wrist and head/egocentric observations with online visual-geometric data quality guidance, and introduces a Gated Egocentric Residual Policy that uses head/egocentric context to correct ambiguous local observations while maintaining stable wrist-view control.
AI.result: Reduces the required number of data episodes, improves data efficiency, and enhances robustness under visual occlusion in real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: EgoGuide improves data efficiency and occlusion robustness in robot learning from demonstrations by combining multimodal egocentric observations with a gated residual policy framework.
